pages.title: Teacher's Guide to This Course
pages.html:
Teacher Reference

Teacher's Guide to This Course

HS Civics: U.S. Government Honors, Grade 11. Master copy, shared across all sections.

This page explains how the course is built, so that every teacher teaching a section is working from the same content, the same sequence, and the same expectations. It is a master copy: it is deliberately not personalized to any one teacher, term, or set of office hours. Add your own contact information and dates in your section's announcements and syllabus, not here.

The built course covers Weeks 1 to 18 across nine numbered Canvas modules: Modules 1–5 (Greco-Roman Foundations through Article I: The Legislative Branch) make up Quarter 1; Modules 6–9 (Article II & III through Civic Duties, Foreign Policy & Comparative Government) make up Quarter 2. The course is fully asynchronous in its Canvas design and is offered in a Live and an On-Demand section; both sections use the same Canvas content and expectations, so there is no separate Live-only or OD-only assignment to keep straight.

How each module and lesson is organized

Every numbered module opens with a Module Opener survey and closes with a Module Closer survey (both ungraded Canvas Quizzes in survey mode). They capture the module's essential question before and after the content, a confidence rating, and a place for students to name what is still unclear. Read them as a set; they are the fastest way to see where a cohort is struggling.

Inside a module, numbered lessons (for example 1.1, 1.2, 1.4…) alternate original instructional pages with primary-source pages. The recurring graded touchpoints around them are:

  • Reading Quiz X.Y: auto-graded multiple choice over the lesson just read, written to require inference rather than lookup.
  • Critical Questions X.Y: a Canvas Discussion tied to a primary source. Per the course's civics standard, every primary-source exercise carries a counterfactual question and a conceptual question, mixed in with others; the category is never named to students, and it should not be named in feedback either.
  • Primary Source Report X.Y: a Canvas Assignment, deeper than a discussion post, over a second primary source in the same lesson pair. This is the module's Tier 3 deep-feedback item alongside Critical Questions.
  • VR activities: most weeks carry solo VR activities that are ungraded or completion-graded. Five weeks (2, 6, 16, 17, 18) each carry one VR activity that is a graded Synchronous Homework & Activities deliverable on top of the standard solo activities. In Module 9, three of these are staged parts of one running project, the Government Systems Portfolio (Beginning, Continuing, Completing), comparing constitutional and authoritarian/communist systems.

Lesson and primary-source pages are not authored in Canvas. Each one is a standalone hosted web page (on the course's GitHub Pages site), embedded into its Canvas page inside an iframe. That is what makes the vocabulary glossary, the hover definitions, and the embedded widgets work; Canvas strips the code that powers them if the content is pasted in directly.

The practical consequence: do not edit lesson text in the Canvas rich content editor. A change made there will look correct until the next deployment overwrites it. Content corrections start in the course build source and flow outward to both the hosted pages and Canvas. Report an error to the course lead rather than patching it in place.

Everything that is graded or teacher-reviewed is Canvas-native: quizzes, assignments, discussions, and the module opener/closer surveys. That split is deliberate. Canvas owns the gradebook and the analytics; the hosted pages own the reading experience.

The four-tier grading architecture

Graded items sit in one of four assignment groups, matching Optima's 500-students-per-teacher design:

Group What lives here
Tier 1: Student & Material Reading Quizzes and other auto-graded or completion items. No grading time.
Tier 2: Student & Community Critical Questions discussions and other light-touch, peer-visible work.
Tier 3: Student & Teacher Primary Source Reports and the two Extended Analysis Projects (one per quarter). These are where a teacher's written feedback matters most.
Tier 4: Ungraded Scaffolding Module Opener/Closer surveys and other ungraded orientation. Costs no grading time but the survey responses are worth reading.

The two Extended Analysis Projects

Each quarter closes with one Extended Analysis Project, a Tier 3 Canvas Assignment with its own Strong/Developing/Beginning rubric:

  • Quarter 1: "From Theory to Text: One Source's Argument in the Constitution," sitting at the end of Module 5, right before the Quarter 1 Practice Exam.
  • Quarter 2: "A Constraint in Practice: Testing a Constitutional Principle Against History," sitting at the end of Module 9, right before the Quarter 2 and Semester Final Practice Exams.

Point values are currently unset by design, not by omission. Both projects carry points_possible: 0 with rubric-based grading turned off, because a prior rubric configuration was silently overriding the intended point total every time the assignment was updated. Rather than guess at a replacement number, the course was left with the point value open for the teacher of record to set. If you are the teacher for this course, set the points before students reach that assignment.

Exams

Three cumulative-by-quarter exam instruments are built into the course, all multiple choice and Canvas-native:

  • Quarter 1 Practice Exam: Modules 1–5, at the end of Module 5.
  • Quarter 2 Practice Exam: Modules 6–9, at the end of Module 9. It covers Quarter 2 only, not the whole year.
  • Semester Final Practice Exam: Modules 1–9, also at the end of Module 9, covering the semester as a whole.

All three are built as ungraded practice quizzes. Whether to convert any of them into a graded quarterly or final exam, and how to weight it against the rest of the gradebook, is a decision for the teacher of record; it has deliberately not been made in the build. There is no Grade 11 Florida Civics EOC (Florida's Civics EOC is administered in Grade 8), so none of these carry EOC-specific tailoring.

Two things to hold to

  • Keep standards codes off student-facing pages. The CPALMS Standards Coverage Matrix lives in this Teacher Module, unpublished, not in anything a student opens. If you find a standards code in a student-facing quiz, assignment, or page, report it as a defect.
  • Do not name the question type to students. Counterfactual and conceptual question types, and tier labels, are for your planning. To the student, a counterfactual question is simply a hard, interesting question, and that is how it should read.

This page may need a follow-up revision. A skill-alignment sweep of this course flagged a set of defects (module wrapper survey data, some page text, a couple of point values) that had not yet been repaired as of this page's writing. If you are revising this course after that remediation lands, re-check the sections above, particularly the Extended Analysis Project point values and the exam list, against the corrected course before trusting this page again.

Questions or corrections go to the course lead so the fix lands in the build source and reaches every section, not just yours.

assignments.title: Walk the Roman Forum: Modeling the Mixed Constitution
assignments.html:
Walk the Roman Forum: Modeling the Mixed Constitution

What You're Doing

This session you have read two ancient theorists (Cicero and Polybius) who each argued that Rome's mixed constitution succeeded because it fused monarchic, aristocratic, and democratic elements into one system that checked itself. That claim is easy to state and easy to forget, because "mixed constitution" is an abstraction until you can point to the actual stones and benches where each element of it operated. In this VR session, you will stand in a reconstruction of the Roman Forum (the physical and political center of the Republic), and use what Polybius and Cicero wrote to identify, arrange, and annotate the spatial evidence of the mixed constitution. The goal is to turn the theory of Lesson 1.14 into something you have walked through and built with your own hands.

What You'll Need
▶
Device: VR headset (recommended for full spatial experience); desktop fallback available if a headset is not accessible.
▶
Session code: [session code assigned by your teacher]
▶
Location: Roman Forum
▶
Before you enter: Have completed Lesson 1.14 and Primary Source 1 (Cicero); Primary Source 2 (Polybius) below should be read before or immediately after this session, since you will cite it in Step 3.
How to Join

Session type: Persistent. This session stays open for the rest of this module, so objects you place and notes you write will remain for you to find again if you re-enter, and may be visible to classmates who enter after you.

1
Launch your VR platform and join the session using the session code [session code assigned by your teacher].
2
You will arrive near the Rostra, the raised speaking platform at the northwest end of the Forum. A note at the starting point restates these steps; check it if you lose your place.
3
From the Rostra, you can see the Curia (Senate House) to your left and the open assembly space stretching out in front of you. Orient yourself before beginning Step 1 below.
What to Do, in Order
1
Observe. Walk to each of the three pre-placed groupings of objects in the Forum: the Curia (Senate House), the Rostra (speaker's platform, where consuls and tribunes addressed the people), and the Consul's Seat (the sella curulis, the ivory folding chair that marked a magistrate holding imperium). Spend a minute at each before moving on.
2
Arrange. Using your VR platform's notes tool, label each of the three locations with the constitutional element it represents: write "Monarchic (Consuls)" and attach it near the Consul's Seat; write "Aristocratic (Senate)" and attach it near the Curia; write "Democratic (Assemblies/Tribunes)" and attach it near the Rostra.
3
Cite. On each of your three notes, add one sentence citing something specific Cicero or Polybius said about that element. For example, your Senate note might quote Cicero's description of aristocracy as rule by "privileged delegates," or Polybius's account of the Senate's role in restraining the consuls; your Consul's Seat note might cite Cicero's description of "a princely and regal power" as one part of the mixed constitution. Use direct language from these primary sources, not just your own paraphrase.
4
Reflect and record. Standing in the center of the Forum where you can see all three locations at once, record a short video (2–3 minutes) in which you explain, out loud, why Polybius believed a constitution combining all three elements resisted the cycle of anacyclosis better than any one of them alone. Refer to the specific locations around you as you speak.
What to Submit

Submit your recording from Step 4 through your VR platform's submission tool, linked to this Canvas assignment. This is your one required submission artifact; your three annotated notes remain in the persistent session as supporting evidence and do not need to be submitted separately.

Time

20–30 minutes.

💡 Teacher Note

This activity asks students to translate an abstract argument (the mixed constitution resists constitutional decay) into a spatial and textual composition they build themselves. The most common sticking point is Step 3: students sometimes write a generic note ("the Senate was powerful") instead of an actual citation from Cicero or Polybius. If you're walking the room, it's worth modeling one citation out loud early (for instance, pointing to the Rostra and reading Polybius's line about the "democratic" element checking oligarchy), so students see what "cite the source" looks like inside a headset, where flipping back to a text is more friction than on paper. Students may want to keep the Primary Source 2 page open on a second device or printed nearby while they work. A finished submission is a short, spoken recording in which the student stands where they can see all three locations and explains the anacyclosis argument in their own words while referring to what's physically around them; it does not need to be polished or scripted.

Success Criteria
▶
Student visited and annotated all three locations (Curia, Rostra, Consul's Seat) with the correct constitutional element.
▶
Each note cites specific language from Cicero or Polybius, not only paraphrase.
▶
Both primary sources (Cicero and Polybius) are referenced across the three notes and the recording.
▶
A recording of 2–3 minutes was submitted through the VR platform's submission tool.

The Convention Floor: Virginia Plan or New Jersey Plan?

This module's graded map assignment is a solo VR Activity. Complete it in one session; it should take about 20–30 minutes once you are inside.

📖 What You're Doing

You have just read how the Virginia Plan and the New Jersey Plan collided in the summer of 1787, and how the Connecticut Compromise finally broke the deadlock between them. In this activity, you will stand on the floor of the Convention itself, read each plan in the words placed there for you, and do the work Roger Sherman's committee actually had to do: decide which specific provisions of each plan are worth keeping, and see how those provisions combine into the bicameral structure the Convention ultimately adopted.

📋 What You'll Need
1
Device: VR headset (recommended) or desktop device.
2
Session code: [insert session code]
3
Location: Independence Hall; Constitutional Convention
4
Completed reading of Lesson 4.2 and Lesson 4.6 before you join.
👥 How to Join

Session type: persistent session. Your placed notes and object arrangement will still be there if you need to leave and come back before submitting.

1
Open your VR platform on your device.
2
Join the session using the session code [insert session code].
3
You will arrive in the Independence Hall; Constitutional Convention location at the marked starting point, facing the Convention floor. A note at the starting point repeats these first steps if you need a reminder once you're inside.
✅ What to Do, In Order
1
Find the two primary-source panels placed on opposite sides of the Convention floor, one labeled Virginia Plan and one labeled New Jersey Plan. Read both panels in full before doing anything else.
2
Using notes, mark at least three provisions from the Virginia Plan and three provisions from the New Jersey Plan that you would keep if you were on Roger Sherman's committee trying to build a compromise. Write a short reason on each note explaining why that provision is worth keeping.
3
Move to the Great Compromise table at the center of the floor. Using the labeled objects provided there (a House group, a Senate group, and a state block for each state), arrange the pieces to represent the bicameral structure the Convention actually adopted; proportional representation in one chamber, equal state representation in the other. Duplicate additional state blocks as needed so every state is represented in both chambers.
4
Stand back from your finished arrangement and record a short video (2–3 minutes) walking through your notes and your final arrangement, explaining in your own words why the structure you built resolves the deadlock between the two plans.
📤 What to Submit

Submit your recording from Step 4 through the Canvas assignment link. Use the video camera object available near the Great Compromise table to capture your walkthrough.

⏳ Time Estimate

20–30 minutes, once you are in the session.

💡 Teacher Note

This activity asks students to translate what they read on Monday and Wednesday into a spatial arrangement they build themselves; the point is not to reproduce the Great Compromise perfectly on the first try, but to reason through why proportional representation and equal state representation can coexist in two different chambers. Students commonly get stuck on the difference between the House group and Senate group arrangement (some students initially duplicate the same number of state blocks into both chambers, missing the point that the House chamber should scale with population while the Senate chamber should not). If you're circulating during a live session, that confusion is worth pausing on directly. Be ready to demonstrate duplicating and locking an object from its control menu for any student who hasn't used those features yet. A finished submission shows six notes with genuine reasoning (not just copied text from the panels) and a recording that correctly explains the population/equality distinction between the two chambers.

From Theory to Text: One Source's Argument in the Constitution
📖 Overview

Across Module 1, you have read a sequence of primary sources spanning over two thousand years: Aristotle and Plutarch on Athens, Polybius and Cicero on Rome, Hobbes, Locke, Montesquieu, and Rousseau on the origins and structure of legitimate authority, Machiavelli on the uses and limits of power, Thomas Paine's Common Sense, the Declaration of Independence, the Federalist Papers, and now the Constitution itself through Article I. None of these sources exists in isolation. Each one argued for a particular theory of legitimate government, and the framers who wrote the Constitution in Philadelphia had read many of them; directly or through the debates they had shaped; before they wrote a single clause.

This project asks you to trace that inheritance directly: to pick up one thread from one source and follow it into the actual words of the Constitution.

📌 Focus Question

How does your chosen source's core argument about legitimate authority show up, and how is it transformed; in the actual text of the U.S. Constitution?

✎ Student Directions
1
Choose one primary source from Module 1 through Module 4 of this module: Aristotle, Cicero, Polybius, Locke, Hobbes, Montesquieu, Rousseau, the Declaration of Independence, Thomas Paine's Common Sense, the Constitution's earlier-studied provisions, Machiavelli, or the Federalist Papers.
2
Identify your source's core argument about what makes political authority legitimate; state it in your own words, in one or two sentences, before you begin drafting.
3
Locate at least two specific clauses or provisions in the Constitution's actual text (you may look beyond Article I to any article you have encountered) where you can show that argument being applied, adapted, or in some cases limited or compromised.

Estimated time: 20–30 minutes, in-headset.

What You're Doing

This session you begin a three-part Government Systems Portfolio that you will carry across the first, second, and third VR sessions. This module's session stands complete on its own; you will examine, judge, and record a full reflection on the civic duty of military service across three American wars, and you'll leave with a real artifact submitted to Canvas. But the whiteboard you build today is also the first panel of a larger portfolio: the next lesson, in the second VR session, you'll return to this same persistent session to add a panel on Cold War foreign policy, and in the third VR session you'll add a final panel comparing constitutional government to the totalitarian systems this course has studied. By the end of the third VR session, you will have a single connected spatial artifact tracing your own reasoning across all three VR sessions.

📡 What You'll Need
▶
Device: VR headset (desktop fallback available for the reading and reflection steps, but the spatial arrangement steps require headset)
▶
Session code: USGH11-W16-[your class section code] (posted in Canvas)
▶
Location: American Homefront: WWII Mobilization
▶
This module's Lesson 9.6 and both primary sources completed beforehand
📡 How to Join

Session type: persistent; this session and everything you place in it will remain available for you to return to in the second and third VR sessions. Join the session using the session code above. You will arrive at the starting point just inside the location; a note there marks the direction to the first primary-source panel.

✅ What to Do, in Order
1
Walk the location and examine the three primary-source panels placed along the main path: a display depicting the 1863 New York City draft riots, an image gallery of WWII enlistment posters, and a display of Vietnam-era draft cards and lottery materials. Read the note beside each panel summarizing the era it represents.
2
Place a whiteboard near the Vietnam-era panel and title it "Government Systems Portfolio." This is the whiteboard you will return to and extend in the second and third VR sessions; treat it as the spine of the whole three-part project.
3
Using notes placed directly on or near each of the three panels, record which era's approach to the civic duty of military service you judge most legitimate, and which you judge least legitimate. Cite specific language or facts from these primary sources (Roosevelt's Pearl Harbor address and Johnson's Johns Hopkins address) in at least one of your notes.
4
On your Government Systems Portfolio whiteboard, write a short summary (3–5 sentences) of your judgment and reasoning from Step 3. Sign it with your name so it is ready for you to build on the next lesson.

Capture one recording (2–4 minutes) walking a viewer through the three panels, your note-based judgments, and your Government Systems Portfolio whiteboard, explaining your reasoning aloud as you go. Upload the recording, or its shareable link, to the VR Activity submission point in Canvas.

20–30 minutes, in-headset.

This activity asks students to render a judgment, not just recall a fact: "most legitimate" and "least legitimate" require the student to weigh the three eras against each other, not just describe them separately. The most common sticking point is Step 3, where students sometimes summarize each panel instead of actually ranking them and defending the ranking with language from Roosevelt or Johnson. If you're circulating, a useful prompt is: "Which of these three approaches to military service would you defend to someone who had to live under it?" Students should have no trouble finding the whiteboard step, since it is a single placed object near the Vietnam-era panel; remind them to sign and date their summary, since they will return to this exact whiteboard in the next two VR sessions. You will visit testimony and memorial content addressing both, extend your whiteboard comparison one final time to set American constitutional government against both totalitarian systems side by side, and close the entire three-part portfolio with a single recording that draws the throughline from the first VR session all the way back to Module 1.

A Constraint in Practice: Testing a Constitutional Principle Against History
📖 Overview

This course has spent a full semester studying constitutional principles designed to limit government power: separation of powers, federalism, judicial review, specific civil liberties and civil rights, and the checks and balances that bind each branch to the others. You have also spent the last module studying what government looks like when those principles are absent altogether; Soviet communism and Nazi totalitarianism, systems that recognized no constitutional limit on the state's power over the individual.

This project asks you to bring both halves of the semester together: to choose one constitutional principle you have studied, and to test it directly against the historical record. Did that principle actually constrain government power in practice, the way it was designed to on paper, and where, if anywhere, did it fall short? You will make this case using primary sources drawn from across the entire semester, and you will sharpen your analysis by holding your chosen principle up against one of the non-constitutional systems this course studied in its final module.

📌 Focus Question

How has your chosen constitutional principle actually functioned, or failed to function; as a real constraint on government power, and what does it look like when a government operates with no such constraint at all?

5
Write an extended essay of 900–1200 words that makes a specific, evidence-based argument about whether and how your chosen principle constrained government power in practice. Quote or cite specific language from your primary sources.
6

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 1.3: Solon and the Birth of Athenian Democracy

questions.text: A Thete (member of Solon's poorest property class) wanted to challenge a magistrate's ruling against him. Under Solon's reforms, what could he do that he could not have done under the previous oligarchy?

answers.text: Run for archonOne of the chief magistrates who governed Athens; before Solon, the office was open only to the hereditary nobility. himself
Appeal the ruling to a jury of fellow citizens
Sell his land to pay off the magistrate
Nothing: the Thetes gained no new rights

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The Thetes remained barred from office-holding, which rules out (a). The right of appeal to a citizen jury was open to every citizen regardless of property class, including the Thetes; this is the reform Aristotle considered most consequential.

questions.text: Before 594 BC, a hektemoros who fell behind on his rent faced which consequence under Athenian law?

answers.text: Exile from Attica
Loss of his right to vote in the Assembly
Enslavement of himself and his family
A fine paid to the AreopagusThe council of former archons that heard serious court cases and guarded the laws of Athens.

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (c). The lesson explains that a debtor's own body served as legal security for the loan; failure to pay could result in the debtor and his family being made bond-servants or sold. This is the practice the Seisachtheia abolished.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the political system of Athens immediately before Solon's archonship?

answers.text: A democracy, because the Assembly already included all citizens
An oligarchy, because office and effective power rested with a narrow landholding aristocracy
A monarchy under a single archonOne of the chief magistrates who governed Athens; before Solon, the office was open only to the hereditary nobility. -for-life
A direct democracy limited to males over sixty

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson defines oligarchy as rule by the few and states that Athenian officers of state were drawn from and remained within the landholding aristocracy before Solon. There is no indication of a single lifetime ruler (ruling out c), and the poor had no reliable political standing at all pre-Solon (ruling out a and d).

questions.text: After completing his reforms, Solon left Athens for ten years. Based on the lesson, what was his stated reason?

answers.text: He had been exiled by the AreopagusThe council of former archons that heard serious court cases and guarded the laws of Athens.
He wanted to prevent either faction from pressuring him to revise his own laws
He needed to raise money as a merchant
The rich had defeated him in a vote and forced him out

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). Both explicit: the lesson states he left "so that no one could pressure him to revise his own laws," having refused offers from both the rich and the poor to become their partisan champion.

questions.text: A student argues: "Solon's Athens was already a full democracy in the modern sense." Based on the lesson, what is the strongest evidence against this claim?

answers.text: Solon cancelled all debts, which no democracy would do
Office-holding still depended on a citizen's property class
Solon refused to leave the city after his reforms
The AreopagusThe council of former archons that heard serious court cases and guarded the laws of Athens. was abolished entirely under Solon

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson is explicit that Solon "did not make Athens a democracy in the sense we would use the word" because office-holding remained tied to the four property classes; the Thetes gained a voice and a vote but not eligibility for office. (a) and (c) misstate the lesson; (d) is not mentioned or true of this period.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 1.11: The Founding of the Republic and the Mixed Constitution

questions.text: Suppose a Roman consul in 500 BC wished to march the army out on a campaign his colleague considered reckless. Based on the lesson, what could that colleague do?

answers.text: Nothing; consuls could not overrule one another once elected
Appeal to the Comitia Centuriata to remove the offending consul
Veto the action, since each consul held full imperium and could forbid the other's act
Ask the Senate to pass a binding law cancelling the campaign

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (c). The lesson states each consul held full imperium and could veto ("I forbid") any act of the other. The Senate's decrees were advisory, not binding law (ruling out d), and removal by the assembly is not described as a check available mid-term (ruling out b).

questions.text: A senator in the early Republic had never been elected by the full citizen body, yet Roman consuls routinely followed the Senate's advice as though it were law. Which best explains why?

answers.text: The Senate held formal veto power over the consuls
Senators were appointed directly by the consuls and owed them personal loyalty
The Senate's authority rested on its members' accumulated experience in office, which no annually rotating consul could match
Roman law required consuls to obey any senatorial decree on penalty of exile

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (c). The lesson explains that senatus consultum were technically advisory, not law, and that the Senate's actual influence came from its being a permanent body of former magistrates whose experience outlasted any single consul's one-year term. Formal veto power belonged to the consuls over each other, not the Senate over the consuls (ruling out a).

questions.text: The lesson contrasts Rome's approach to checking power with Athens's approach. Which pairing correctly matches each city with its primary strategy?

answers.text: Athens: institutional plurality; Rome: direct citizen power
Athens: direct citizen power; Rome: institutional plurality
Both cities relied primarily on property-weighted assemblies
Both cities relied primarily on a single supreme magistrate

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states Athens widened the circle of direct citizen participation (following Solon and Cleisthenes, studied in Module 1), while Rome multiplied and divided offices against one another. Neither city fits (c) or (d) as its primary strategy.

questions.text: In the Comitia Centuriata, wealthy citizens were a small minority of the voting population but frequently decided the outcome of a vote before poorer citizens had finished casting theirs. What does this reveal about the assembly's structure?

answers.text: Voting blocs were weighted by property and rank, not by simple headcount
Only the wealthy were permitted to vote at all
The assembly's votes were purely advisory, like the Senate's
Poorer citizens voted in a separate, powerless assembly

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (a). The lesson states the assembly organized citizens into blocs weighted toward property and military rank, so fewer wealthy citizens controlled enough blocs to decide questions ahead of the more numerous but lower-weighted blocs. The lesson does not state that only the wealthy could vote (ruling out b) or that this assembly's votes were advisory (ruling out c).

questions.text: A student argues: "Rome in 509 BC was already a democracy in the way Athens became one after Cleisthenes." Based on the lesson, what is the strongest evidence against this claim?

answers.text: Rome had no popular assemblies at all
The consuls held office for life, unlike any Athenian magistrate
Rome's assemblies existed but weighted votes toward property and rank rather than toward equal citizen headcount
The Senate was elected annually by the whole citizen body

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (c). The lesson is explicit that the res publica depended on citizen consent through the assemblies, but that the dominant note in the early Republic was checked plurality among offices, not equal-weight popular rule; the Comitia Centuriata weighted voting toward wealth and rank. (a), (b), and (d) all misstate facts given in the lesson; assemblies existed, consuls served one-year terms, and the Senate was not elected by the whole citizen body.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 2.3: Hobbes and the War of All Against All
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts from the lesson. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: A modest person in Hobbes's state of nature, who genuinely wants only to live quietly and take nothing from anyone, still finds it rational to consider striking first against a stranger. Based on the lesson, why?

answers.text: Because Hobbes believes all people are naturally cruel
Because he cannot know whether the stranger is equally modest, and the cost of guessing wrong is too high, given no common power to protect him
Because the laws of nature command preemptive violence
Because property does not yet exist, so there is nothing to lose by attacking

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explains diffidence as rational distrust arising from uncertainty about others' intentions combined with the absence of any authority to enforce safety; this holds even for people who mean no harm, which rules out (a) and (c). Property's absence (d) is a consequence of the war, not its cause.

questions.text: Hobbes says the state of nature is a state of "war," but also says people are not necessarily fighting every moment. How does the lesson reconcile these two claims?

answers.text: Hobbes contradicts himself and the lesson does not resolve it
War for Hobbes means only large-scale organized battles between armies
War describes a constant disposition or threat of violence, similar to how bad weather can describe a standing inclination toward rain rather than rain itself
The state of nature is only a state of war after the social contract is broken

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (c). The lesson uses Hobbes's own weather analogy to explain that "war" names the ever-present disposition to violence, not continuous fighting. (d) reverses the order of Hobbes's argument, since the contract is what ends the state of nature, not what begins the war within it.

questions.text: Which of the following best explains why the state-of-nature method counts as a "revolution" in how people argued about political legitimacy, according to the lesson?

answers.text: It was the first time anyone had written about government
It replaced appeals to inherited custom or divine right with an argument built from reasoning about human nature, available to anyone willing to think it through
It proved that monarchy was illegitimate in every case
It was based on direct observation of real societies without government

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explicitly contrasts this method with Filmer's appeal to inherited authority from Adam, framing the shift as reasoning from first principles rather than tradition. (c) overclaims; Hobbes's method in fact defends near-absolute sovereignty; (d) is wrong since the state of nature is explicitly described as imagined, not observed.

questions.text: A student argues: "Since the social contract is supposed to protect people from harm, subjects should be able to remove a sovereign who treats them badly." Based on Hobbes's actual reasoning as described in the lesson, why would Hobbes reject this?

answers.text: Because Hobbes believes all sovereigns are naturally good and would never mistreat subjects
Because allowing subjects to judge and resist the sovereign would return to each individual the very power to judge their own case that caused the war of all against all in the first place
Because the social contract legally cannot be enforced once signed
Because Hobbes did not believe governments needed subjects' consent at all

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). This connects two ideas from the lesson: the original cause of the war of all against all (everyone judging their own case) and Hobbes's reasoning for why a right of rebellion would recreate that same condition. (d) is contradicted by the lesson's description of the contract as arising from rational consent.

questions.text: Based on the lesson's closing paragraph, what should a student expect to be the central point of comparison when Locke is introduced later this session?

answers.text: Whether a state of nature and social contract exist at all
Whether the social contract, once made, can ever be broken or is instead final and irreversible
Whether human beings are naturally equal
Whether government should have a legislature

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explicitly flags that Locke shares Hobbes's tools (state of nature, social contract, reasoning from first principles) but reaches a different conclusion specifically about whether authority can run out; making this the hinge of this comparison, not the more general questions in (a) or (c), which both thinkers would answer similarly.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 2.11: Montesquieu and the Separation of Powers
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts from the lesson. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: A small nation has one governing council that both writes all statutes and personally carries out arrests and punishments under those statutes. According to Montesquieu's argument, what specific danger does this arrangement create?

answers.text: The council will be too slow to respond to emergencies
The council can write tyrannical laws and then enforce them without restraint, since no other body checks either function
The council will lack the legal authority to punish anyone at all
The people will have no representatives in the council

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explains that when legislative and executive power are united in one body, that body faces no external check on writing self-serving laws or on how harshly it enforces them; Montesquieu's own words are that such a body "should enact tyrannical laws, to execute them in a tyrannical manner." (a), (c), and (d) are not claims the lesson makes.

questions.text: Montesquieu writes that if judicial power is joined to the legislative power, "the judge would be then the legislator." Based on the lesson's explanation of this line, what is he warning against?

answers.text: Judges deciding cases too slowly
Lawmakers effectively rewriting the law case-by-case under the guise of judging, rather than applying a law that already exists
Judges being paid a legislative salary
Legislatures having too few members to hear cases

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explains that a lawmaking body that also judges is not applying a pre-existing law neutrally; it is deciding, case by case, what the law means for a specific person, which the lesson describes as "legislating after the fact, dressed up as judging."

questions.text: The lesson contrasts Montesquieu's idealized England with Turkey and the aristocratic republics of Italy. What do Turkey and the Italian republics have in common, according to Montesquieu's argument, despite one being a monarchy and the others being aristocracies?

answers.text: Both have no executive power at all
Both concentrate all three powers in a single person or body, producing oppression regardless of how many people hold that power
Both have juries drawn from ordinary citizens
Both separate the judiciary from the legislature completely

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states that concentration of power "produces the same disease whether the concentration sits in one man or in one committee"; Turkey concentrates all three powers in the sultan, the Italian republics concentrate them in a single aristocratic body, and both result in oppression despite the different number of people holding power.

questions.text: According to the lesson, what specific tool does Montesquieu's idealized English executive hold over the legislature, and what tool does the legislature hold over the executive in return?

answers.text: The executive can dissolve the legislature permanently; the legislature can remove the executive by simple vote
The executive can reject legislation without writing it; the legislature controls funding, keeping the executive dependent on it
The executive appoints all judges; the legislature appoints all executive ministers
Neither power has any tool over the other; they are fully isolated

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explicitly describes the executive's veto ("reject legislation...without being able to write it") and the legislature's power of the purse ("an executive dependent on annual funding cannot become independent of the legislature that grants it") as the specific reciprocal checks in Montesquieu's model. (d) contradicts the lesson's point that separation is "not total isolation."

questions.text: A student claims: "Montesquieu's main worry is that bad or foolish people might end up running the government." Based on the lesson's opening argument, why is this an inaccurate summary of his position?

answers.text: Montesquieu believed most rulers throughout history were, in fact, good people
Montesquieu's argument is structural: even a genuinely good ruler will tend to abuse unchecked power, so the solution is arranging power itself, not selecting better people
Montesquieu never discusses the character of rulers at all
Montesquieu believed only elected rulers could be trusted with power

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson opens with Montesquieu's refusal to accept that staffing government with good people solves the problem, quoting his claim that "every man invested with power is apt to abuse it" and that "virtue itself has need of limits." His remedy is structural (power checking power), not a claim about who should hold office.

quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts from the lesson. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: A colonist in the fall of 1774 supported the First Continental Congress's petition to the king but would likely have opposed the idea of independence. Based on the lesson, why is this position historically consistent, rather than contradictory?

answers.text: The First Congress had already voted for independence, so no consistent colonist could oppose it
The First Congress explicitly sought reconciliation with the Crown, not separation, so supporting its petition did not commit anyone to independence
Independence was not debated at all until after the war ended
The First Congress was organized specifically to plan for war with Britain

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states the First Continental Congress petitioned the king and affirmed its desire for reconciliation, not rupture. Supporting that petition was compatible with continued loyalty to the Crown; independence was a separate, later question.

questions.text: By the winter of 1775–76, the Second Continental Congress found itself in what the lesson calls an "untenable position." Which combination of facts explains why?

answers.text: It was managing a war while still professing loyalty to a king who had declared the colonies in rebellion
It had already declared independence but had no army to defend it
It had disbanded the Continental Army after Lexington and Concord
George III had personally apologized for the Coercive Acts

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (a). The lesson explains that Congress was raising and directing an army and fighting an actual war, yet still professing loyalty to the Crown and hoping for reconciliation; a position made impossible when George III refused the Olive Branch Petition and declared the colonies in rebellion.

questions.text: According to the lesson, what specific rhetorical problem did Thomas Paine's Common Sense solve for colonists in January 1776 that a decade of arguments about taxation had not solved?

answers.text: It proved Parliament had overstepped on a specific tax
It opened a legitimate third political position (self-governing independence) between loyal subject and outlaw traitor, by attacking the legitimacy of monarchy itself
It convinced Congress to send another petition to the king
It was the first document to mention natural rights

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states that before Paine, the only two visible options were loyal subject or treasonous outlaw. questions.text: The Declaration's long list of charges against George III (the "He has…" section) is structurally compared in the lesson to a legal indictment. Based on the lesson's explanation of the document's three-part architecture, what specific job does this section do that the opening paragraph's theory of government cannot do by itself?

answers.text: It states the formal declaration of separation
It supplies evidence that the conditions Locke's theory requires for legitimate rebellion (a deliberate, sustained pattern of abuse aimed at absolute despotism) have actually been met
It summarizes the Olive Branch Petition
It repeats the natural rights argument in different words

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson is explicit that theory (part one) supplies the standard for legitimate rebellion, while the indictment (part two) supplies the proof that this particular government has met that standard through a "long train of abuses" pursued deliberately.

questions.text: John Adams complained that the Declaration contained "not an idea. . . but what had been hackneyed in Congress for two years before," and Jefferson agreed this was substantially true. Based on the lesson, what does this fact imply about the actual source of the Declaration's power and persuasiveness?

answers.text: The Declaration was powerful because it introduced a wholly new and unfamiliar political philosophy to Americans
The Declaration failed to persuade anyone because it lacked original ideas
The Declaration's power came not from novelty but from stating clearly and persuasively a Lockean theory of government already widely shared among educated Americans by 1776
Adams's complaint proves the Declaration plagiarized Common Sense

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (c). The lesson states directly that the Declaration's power was never that it said something no one had thought before, but that it expressed, with clarity and felicity, ideas that had already become close to commonplace among Americans through Locke and Whig political culture.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 4.3: Philadelphia, 1787: Madison's Convention
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts from the lesson. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: The delegates who traveled to Philadelphia in May 1787 had been formally instructed by their states to do what?

answers.text: Draft an entirely new constitution from scratch
Revise the Articles of Confederation
Elect a president to replace Congress
Negotiate a peace treaty with Britain

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states the delegates' official charge was to revise the Articles of Confederation so the existing government could function; nothing in their instructions authorized writing a new constitution, which is precisely why the Convention's decision to do so was audacious.

questions.text: A small-state delegate at the Convention would most likely have supported which plan, and why?

answers.text: The Virginia Plan, because it gave every state one vote regardless of population
The New Jersey Plan, because it preserved equal state representation in a single-chamber Congress
The Virginia Plan, because it apportioned both legislative houses by population
Neither plan, because both abolished the states entirely

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explains that small states feared being permanently outvoted under population-based representation, and that the New Jersey Plan kept the Articles' one-state-one-vote structure while adding new federal powers; making it the plan built to protect small-state equality. (a) and (c) describe the Virginia Plan inaccurately or attribute the wrong feature to it.

questions.text: Based on the lesson's account of Madison's preparation, what specific insight from his study of ancient and modern confederacies most directly shaped the Virginia Plan's design?

answers.text: Confederacies fail because they lack a strong national capital city
Confederacies fail when they cannot act directly on individual citizens, relying instead on voluntary state cooperation
Confederacies fail because they always favor large states over small ones
Confederacies fail whenever they include more than thirteen members

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states Madison's research convinced him that without a way to act directly on individual citizens rather than merely requesting state cooperation, a confederacy has no real government; this is the diagnosis that drove the Virginia Plan's proposal of a national government answerable to the people rather than the states.

questions.text: Why does the lesson credit Madison as the "Father of the Constitution" despite noting that he lost several arguments over the summer and did not write every clause?

answers.text: He personally signed the Constitution before any other delegate
His preparatory framework set the Convention's starting terms of debate more than any other delegate's did
He was elected president of the Convention
He was the only delegate who supported the New Jersey Plan

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson is explicit that the title reflects Madison's outline becoming the Convention's starting proposal and his framework setting the terms of debate from the opening days, not perfect authorship or unbroken success in every argument.

questions.text: A student claims: "Shays' Rebellion and the Annapolis Convention were unrelated events that happened to occur around the same time." Based on the lesson, what is the strongest evidence against this claim?

answers.text: Both events took place in Philadelphia
The Annapolis Convention's call for a broader convention created the opening that the alarm over Shays' Rebellion then helped push a critical mass of states to accept
Shays' Rebellion was the direct cause of the Annapolis Convention
Neither event had any connection to the Constitutional Convention

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson presents Annapolis (September 1786) as the event that first proposed a broader convention, and Shays' Rebellion (winter 1786) as the shock that then convinced a critical mass of statesmen the confederation could not keep the peace; together, not separately, driving states to send delegates to Philadelphia. (c) reverses the actual chronology and causal relationship.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 4.11: Publius Writes for New York
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts from the lesson. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: A classmate says, "The Federalist Papers are a neutral, scholarly explanation of what the Constitution means." Based on the lesson, what is the strongest evidence against this claim?

answers.text: Publius was a single real person, not a pen name
Hamilton and Madison had been delegates at Philadelphia and had a direct stake in ratification
The essays were published after New York had already ratified the Constitution
John Jay wrote all eighty-five essays alone

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explains that Hamilton and Madison helped write the Constitution at Philadelphia and were arguing for a document they already believed should pass; advocacy aimed at a specific skeptical audience, not disinterested commentary. (a) and (d) misstate who Publius was; (c) reverses the actual timing, since the essays were written to persuade the convention before its vote.

questions.text: Madison defines a faction as a group united by a common passion or interest adverse to others' rights or the community's good. Based on that definition, which of the following could count as a faction?

answers.text: Only a minority group with no political power
Only a group that breaks the law
Either a minority or a majority, provided its shared aim works against others' rights or the common good
Only groups organized around religion

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (c). The lesson quotes Madison's definition directly: a faction may amount to "a majority or minority of the whole." Size is not the defining feature; the adverse relationship to others' rights or the aggregate community interest is. (a), (b), and (d) each wrongly narrow the definition.

questions.text: Madison rejects "removing the causes" of faction by destroying liberty. Why, according to the lesson, does he treat this option as worse than the problem it would solve?

answers.text: Because destroying liberty is illegal under the Articles of Confederation
Because liberty is the very condition that makes faction possible, so eliminating it would eliminate free political life itself
Because the states would never agree to give up liberty
Because factions are actually good for republics and should be preserved

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explains Madison's fire/air analogy: liberty is to faction what air is to fire, an aliment without which it cannot exist, so removing liberty to stop faction would be curing the disease by killing the patient. (a) and (c) are not mentioned; (d) misreads Madison, who calls faction a "dangerous vice," not a good.

questions.text: Based on the lesson's comparison between Madison and Rousseau, which best describes how Madison's argument responds to Rousseau's idea of the general will?

answers.text: Madison agrees that a small, direct democracy is safest from faction
Madison argues that keeping a community small and direct actually makes majority faction more dangerous, not less
Madison never considered the question of community size
Madison thinks the general will and the extended republic are the same idea

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states that Madison treats Rousseau's small, direct model as "a description of the exact conditions under which faction becomes most dangerous," since nothing checks a factious majority once it controls a small assembly directly. (a) reverses Madison's actual claim; (c) and (d) are not supported by the lesson.

questions.text: A pure democracy, in Madison's sense, and an extended republic differ chiefly in size and in the presence of representation. Based on the lesson, why does greater size make majority faction less likely to succeed?

answers.text: Larger territories have more police to enforce the law
A greater variety of interests makes it harder for a single common motive to unite a majority and for that majority to coordinate
Representatives are paid more in larger republics and so are less corruptible
Size has no effect on faction; only the type of government matters

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson quotes Madison directly: extending the sphere "take[s] in a greater variety of parties and interests," making a common majority motive less likely and, if it exists, harder to coordinate. (a) and (c) are not mentioned; (d) contradicts the lesson's central point about scale.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 4.19: Hamilton and the Problem of Choosing a President
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts from the lesson. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: A delegate in 1787 objects to direct national popular election of the president on the grounds that voters in one state cannot evaluate a candidate from a distant state. Based on the lesson, what feature of late-eighteenth-century America made this objection especially serious?

answers.text: The Constitution did not yet permit interstate travel
No national newspapers or media existed to inform citizens across long distances quickly
Most states did not allow any citizens to vote at all
The president was expected to serve for life

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explains that no national media network existed and that communication across states took days or weeks, making it practically impossible for voters to verify a distant candidate's fitness for office. (a), (c), and (d) are not stated or true of the period.

questions.text: The convention also rejected having Congress select the president outright. Based on the lesson, what specific danger did this option pose that direct popular election did not?

answers.text: Congress had no way to communicate with the states
It risked making the president dependent on and obliging toward the legislature, undermining separation of powers
It would have been unconstitutional under the Articles of Confederation
It would have excluded small states from having any voice in the choice

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states that a president chosen and reappointed by Congress would have incentive to become "Congress's creature," collapsing the independence of the executive branch from the legislative. (a), (c), and (d) are not supported by the lesson.

questions.text: According to the lesson, why did Hamilton consider it an advantage that electors met and voted separately within their own states rather than all assembling in one place?

answers.text: It made the process faster
It reduced the chance that electors would be swept along by a single collective wave of passion or disorder
It guaranteed that every state's electors would vote the same way
It allowed electors to serve for life

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explains that Hamilton saw the electors' "detached and divided situation" as minimizing tumult and disorder compared to a single assembled body voting all at once. (a), (c), and (d) are not part of Hamilton's stated reasoning.

questions.text: Based on the lesson, why would a small, permanent council of electors have been more vulnerable to foreign corruption than the system Hamilton describes?

answers.text: A permanent, standing body offers a stable, identifiable target that a foreign power has time to bribe or influence; temporary, dispersed electors do not
Permanent councils are always composed of foreign-born citizens
The Constitution required permanent councils to publish their votes in advance
Foreign powers were legally permitted to appoint electors directly

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (a). The lesson connects Hamilton's concern about "cabal, intrigue, and corruption" to the electors' temporary, decentralized character, which denies a foreign agent the standing, bribable target a permanent body would present. (b), (c), and (d) are invented and unsupported.

questions.text: A student claims: "The Electoral College works exactly the same way today as Hamilton described it in 1788." Based on the lesson, what historical development contradicts this claim?

answers.text: Electors are now chosen by the Supreme Court
The rise of political parties led states to select electors pledged in advance to a party's ticket, rather than independent deliberators
The Constitution was amended to eliminate the Electoral College entirely
Electors no longer vote at all

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explicitly states that within decades of the founding, the rise of parties changed elector selection toward pledged party loyalists rather than the independent deliberators Hamilton envisioned. (a), (c), and (d) are false statements not found in the lesson.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 5.3: A Congress of Two Minds
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions drawn from Lesson 9.1 and the Constitution excerpt. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: A bill has just passed the House of Representatives after a wave of sudden public anger over a single news event. Based on the lesson's description of institutional temperament, what would you predict about how the Senate is likely to handle that same bill?

answers.text: The Senate will pass it just as quickly, since both chambers respond to public opinion at the same speed
The Senate is more likely to slow the bill down, since its longer terms and staggered elections were designed to insulate it from short-term public pressure
The Senate cannot consider a bill the House has already passed
The Senate will automatically reject any bill motivated by public anger

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explains that the House's two-year terms make it responsive to immediate public sentiment, while the Senate's six-year, staggered terms were designed to insulate it from exactly that kind of short-term pressure. (c) and (d) are not supported anywhere in the lesson; (a) contradicts the lesson's central contrast.

questions.text: Under the Constitution as originally ratified in 1788, a state's two Senators would have been chosen by which of the following?

answers.text: A direct statewide popular vote, the same as Representatives
The state legislature
The Governor alone
The Electoral College

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). Article I, Section 3 states Senators were "chosen by the Legislature thereof." The lesson notes this changed only with the Seventeenth Amendment in 1913, which the student must connect to recognize that direct popular election (a) was not the original method.

questions.text: The President has negotiated a treaty with a foreign nation. Based on the lesson, what must happen before that treaty binds the United States?

answers.text: A simple majority of the full Congress, House and Senate together, must approve it
Two-thirds of the Senators present must consent to it
The House of Representatives must ratify it, since all matters of national import begin there
No further approval is needed once the President signs it

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states the Senate's advice-and-consent power over treaties requires a two-thirds vote of Senators present. The House plays no formal ratifying role in treaties, ruling out (a) and (c); the President's signature alone is not sufficient, ruling out (d).

questions.text: Based on the lesson's explanation of why the Senate, rather than the House, received the treaty and ambassador-confirmation powers, which of the following best states the framers' underlying reasoning?

answers.text: The House was considered too small to handle complex negotiations

Foreign policy required the kind of continuity, discretion, and insulation from rapid electoral turnover that the Senate's design provided, while the House's speed made it ill-suited to this specific task
The framers believed foreign policy was unimportant compared to domestic legislation
The Senate demanded these powers as a condition of ratifying the Constitution

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explicitly ties the Senate's staggered terms, institutional memory, and insulation from rapid public pressure to why it was judged the right chamber for treaty-making and ambassador confirmation. (a), (c), and (d) are not supported by the lesson.

questions.text: A student claims: "Declaring war and ratifying a treaty are handled by the same part of Congress, for the same reasons." Based on the lesson, what is the strongest evidence against this claim?

answers.text: Declarations of war require the full Congress, including the House, because the framers wanted the decision to start a war made slowly with the people's most direct representatives involved, while treaty ratification is a Senate-only power reflecting a different set of design priorities
The Constitution does not mention declaring war at all
Only the President can declare war, so the comparison is meaningless
Treaties do not require any congressional involvement

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (a). The Three-Fifths Compromise, since it concerns apportionment
No basis exists, since Congress may only exercise powers listed word-for-word
The treaty power, since copyright involves foreign nations

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (a). The lesson explains the Necessary and Proper Clause grants Congress authority to choose the means of executing an already-enumerated power (here, the "Science and useful Arts" / authors-and-inventors clause), not an entirely new independent power. questions.text: Under the Three-Fifths Compromise, how did a state's slave population affect that state's power in the House of Representatives?

Slaves were excluded entirely, giving slaveholding states no additional House seats for them

Three-fifths of a state's total slave population was added to its free population for apportionment, increasing a slaveholding state's number of House seats without giving the slave population itself any vote
Slaves could vote by proxy through their owners

Declaring war on any nation that practiced the slave trade
Amending the Constitution in any way

questions.text: A student argues: "The 1808 date in the slave-trade clause proves the framers had never thought about restricting the slave trade before the Constitutional Convention." Based on the lesson, what is the strongest evidence against this claim?

answers.text: The 1774 Continental Association already included a pledge to halt the slave trade, and several states had independently restricted or banned slave importation in the 1770s and 1780s, well before 1787
The Constitution was written in a single afternoon with no prior debate
No American colony ever discussed the slave trade before 1808
The framers were legally required by Britain to keep the trade open

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (a). (b), (c), and (d) are unsupported or false.

questions.text: Based on the lesson, which of the following best describes what happened after Congress banned the importation of slaves effective January 1, 1808?

The ban had no effect of any kind and was never enforced
New importation from abroad stopped, but slavery itself continued, sustained by the existing slave population, for decades until the Thirteenth Amendment
The ban was ruled unconstitutional by the Supreme Court within a year

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (c). The lesson is explicit that the 1808 law stopped new arrivals from abroad but did not end slavery, which persisted for fifty-seven more years until the Thirteenth Amendment. (a), (b), and (d) all contradict the lesson directly.
