quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 6.3: The President's Job Description
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts from the lesson. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: A 33-year-old naturalized citizen who has lived in the United States for twenty years wants to run for President. Based on the lesson, why would this person be constitutionally ineligible?

answers.text: They fail the residency requirement
They fail both the age requirement and the natural-born-citizen requirement
They fail only the age requirement
There is no constitutional barrier; only political parties can exclude candidates

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states a President must be at least thirty-five (this candidate is thirty-three) and a natural-born citizen (this candidate is naturalized, not natural-born). The fourteen-year residency requirement is satisfied by twenty years, ruling out (a).

questions.text: Based on the lesson's explanation of the Take Care Clause, which of the following best describes the constitutional theory of the President's core job?

answers.text: The President writes law and Congress carries it out
Congress writes law and the President's assigned constitutional task is to see it faithfully executed
The President and Congress share the job of writing law equally, with no distinction between them
The Take Care Clause gives the President authority to ignore laws he disagrees with

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states the Take Care Clause requires the President to "take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed," and explicitly frames this as Congress writing law while the President's job is administering and enforcing it, not rewriting it.

questions.text: The President wants to appoint a new federal judge and negotiate a treaty with a foreign government in the same month. Based on the lesson, what do both actions have in common procedurally?

answers.text: Both require a two-thirds vote of the full Congress
Both require the Senate's advice and consent, though the appointment needs only a majority while the treaty needs two-thirds
Neither requires any involvement from Congress
Both require approval from the House of Representatives specifically

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states appointments require Senate confirmation by simple majority in practice, while treaties require two-thirds of Senators present; both are Senate-only advice-and-consent powers, with different thresholds. The House plays no formal role in either, ruling out (a) and (d).

questions.text: A student claims: "Article II gives the President complete, independent control over war and foreign affairs, with no role for Congress at all." Based on the lesson, what is the strongest evidence against this claim?

answers.text: The President is commander-in-chief, but declaring war belongs to Congress, and treaties require Senate consent by a two-thirds vote
The Constitution does not mention the military at all
The President cannot receive foreign ambassadors under any circumstances
Congress must approve every troop movement in advance

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (a). The lesson explicitly notes that command of the military does not include the power to declare the war it might fight (that belongs to Congress, per Module 5), and that treaties require Senate consent. (b), (c), and (d) all misstate facts given in the lesson.

questions.text: A President who has already won two elected terms wants to run for a third. Based on the lesson, which amendment would prevent this today, and what does the lesson say about the norm that amendment replaced?

answers.text: The Twelfth Amendment, which had always legally limited Presidents to two terms
The Twenty-Second Amendment, which formally limited Presidents to two elected terms after Franklin Roosevelt broke a two-term norm every prior President had followed voluntarily
The Twentieth Amendment, which sets the inauguration date
The Twenty-Fifth Amendment, which governs presidential succession

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states the Twenty-Second Amendment (1951) codified the two-term limit after Roosevelt won a third and fourth term, breaking a voluntary norm dating to Washington. The Twelfth Amendment concerns Electoral College voting procedure, the Twentieth concerns the inauguration date, and the Twenty-Fifth concerns succession and disability; none of them address term limits.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 6.7: The Veto and Federalist No. 70
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions drawn from Lesson 10.2 and the Federalist No. 70 excerpt above. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: Congress passes a bill and sends it to the President with nine days left in its session. The President takes no action and Congress adjourns before the ten days are up. Based on the lesson, what happens to the bill?

answers.text: It automatically becomes law without his signature
It dies through a pocket veto, since Congress adjourned before the ten-day window closed and he never signed it
Congress must immediately reconvene to vote on an override
The bill is sent to the Supreme Court for review

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson defines the pocket veto as exactly this scenario: Congress adjourns within ten days of sending the bill, the President takes no action, and the bill dies automatically without a formal veto message. (a) describes what happens if Congress remains in session and ten days pass, not this scenario.

questions.text: Based on the lesson, why does overriding a regular veto require a two-thirds vote in both chambers rather than a simple majority?

answers.text: The Constitution requires a two-thirds vote for all ordinary legislation
The higher threshold, like the Senate's two-thirds treaty requirement, is meant to require broad, cross-partisan consensus before overruling the executive's objection
A simple majority would violate the Take Care Clause
The framers wanted overrides to be functionally impossible

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explicitly draws the parallel to the Senate's two-thirds treaty threshold from Module 5, framing both as deliberately set above a bare majority to require broader consensus. (a) misstates ordinary legislative procedure, which requires only a simple majority to pass initially.

questions.text: A student claims: "The veto lets the President write his own version of a law when he disagrees with Congress." Based on the lesson, what is the strongest evidence against this claim?

answers.text: The veto is not a lawmaking power; a vetoed bill that fails an override simply does not become law, rather than being replaced by the President's preferred text
The President cannot use the veto more than once per year
Only the Senate can veto legislation
Vetoed bills automatically pass regardless of Congress's response

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (a). The lesson states directly that the President "cannot write a bill's language" and that a vetoed, non-overridden bill "simply fails to become law rather than being replaced with the President's preferred version." (b), (c), and (d) are not supported by the lesson.

questions.text: Based on Hamilton's argument in the Federalist No. 70 excerpt, what does he claim actually happened to Rome's divided executive during its worst crises?

answers.text: The consuls governed even more effectively together under pressure
Rome had to abandon its divided executive and take refuge in the absolute power of a single Dictator
The Senate replaced the consuls permanently
Rome adopted a three-person executive to resolve consular disputes

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The excerpt states Rome was "obliged to take refuge in the absolute power of a single man, under the formidable title of Dictator" during crises; evidence Hamilton uses against the reliability of a divided executive. (a), (c), and (d) are not supported by the excerpt.

questions.text: Combining Lesson 6.5 and the Federalist No. 70 excerpt, why did the American framers reject Rome's dual-consul model for the presidency, according to Hamilton's argument?

answers.text: They believed a single executive would produce more decisive, accountable government, since dividing power invited the kind of "dissensions" and diffused responsibility Hamilton attributes to Rome's consuls and Decemvirs
They had never heard of the Roman consulship
They wanted the presidency to be as weak as possible
Hamilton argued Rome's dual consulship worked perfectly and should be copied exactly

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (a). The lesson and excerpt together show Hamilton using Rome's consular "dissensions" and the Decemvirs' concentrated danger as evidence for unity, arguing a single executive produces "decision, activity, secrecy, and despatch" that a divided one cannot. (d) directly contradicts Hamilton's critical reading of Roman history.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 6.10: One Supreme Court and Whatever Congress Builds Beneath It
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts from the lesson. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: A member of Congress proposes abolishing every federal circuit court of appeals in the country. Based on the lesson, could Congress constitutionally do this to the Supreme Court itself the same way?

answers.text: Yes, Congress created every federal court including the Supreme Court and can abolish any of them
No, the Constitution itself establishes the Supreme Court directly, while circuit courts exist only because Congress chose to create them under its Article III discretion
No, only a constitutional amendment can change any federal court's caseload
Yes, but only if the President agrees in advance

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states Article III vests judicial power "in one supreme Court" directly, while "inferior" courts exist only because Congress "ordained and established" them under its own discretion. Congress could restructure lower courts (as it has repeatedly since 1789), but the Supreme Court's existence comes from the Constitution's own text, not from a congressional statute like the courts below it.

questions.text: A newly elected Congress is frustrated with a federal judge's rulings and proposes cutting that judge's salary by half until he retires. Based on the lesson, what specific Article III protection would this violate?

answers.text: The good behaviour tenure protection, since salary and tenure are the same guarantee
Nothing; Congress controls appropriations and may set any judge's pay
The protection against diminishing a judge's compensation during his continuance in office
The jury trial guarantee

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (c). The lesson distinguishes two separate protections: good behaviour tenure (removal only by impeachment) and salary protection (compensation "shall not be diminished during their Continuance in Office"). Cutting pay to pressure a judge targets the salary protection specifically, which the lesson ties directly to Hamilton's Federalist No. 78 argument from Module 4 that Congress must not be able to leverage a judge's pay against his independence.

questions.text: Ohio sues Kentucky directly in a dispute over their shared border along the Ohio River, with no lower court involved. Based on the lesson, what kind of jurisdiction allows the Supreme Court to hear this case first, as a trial?

answers.text: Appellate jurisdiction, because state disputes always start at the circuit court level
Original jurisdiction, because Article III gives the Supreme Court authority to hear certain cases, including state-versus-state disputes, as the very first court
No jurisdiction; states cannot sue each other under Article III
Concurrent jurisdiction shared equally with Congress

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson's concrete example is exactly this scenario: a direct state-versus-state dispute goes straight to the Supreme Court because Article III places controversies "in which a State shall be Party" within the Court's original jurisdiction, meaning no lower court hears it first.

questions.text: A defendant convicted of a federal crime in district court loses an appeal at the circuit court of appeals and wants the Supreme Court to review the case. Based on the lesson, why is this appellate jurisdiction rather than original jurisdiction, and what is the Supreme Court actually reviewing at this stage?

answers.text: It is original jurisdiction, since the Supreme Court is the only court that matters
It is appellate jurisdiction because a lower court already decided the case first, and the Supreme Court reviews whether the law was applied correctly rather than retrying the facts from scratch
It is appellate jurisdiction, but the Supreme Court must re-hear all the original testimony as if for the first time
Criminal cases can never reach the Supreme Court under Article III

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson's criminal-appeal example matches this exactly: appellate jurisdiction applies because a district court and circuit court already ruled, and the lesson states the Court "is not retrying the facts from scratch in this posture; it is reviewing whether the law was applied correctly below."

questions.text: A political leader accuses a rival of treason simply for publicly criticizing a government policy, with no evidence of war or aid to an enemy. Based on the lesson, why would this accusation fail under Article III?

answers.text: Treason charges require a jury trial only, with no other restriction

Article III defines treason narrowly as levying war or giving aid and comfort to enemies, and requires two witnesses to the same overt act or a courtroom confession; criticism alone satisfies neither the definition nor the evidence standard
The Constitution does not define treason at all, leaving it entirely to Congress
Treason can only be charged against foreign nationals, not citizens

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states Article III defines treason narrowly ("levying War," or "adhering to their Enemies, giving them Aid and Comfort") and requires either two witnesses to the same overt act or an open-court confession, explaining this was a deliberate guard against the loose treason accusations the framers had seen the English Crown use against political opponents. Mere criticism meets neither the definition nor the evidentiary bar.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 6.14: Judicial Review and Federalist No. 78
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions drawn from Lesson 11.2 and the Federalist No. 78 excerpt above. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: A student searches Article III's full text for the phrase "judicial review" and cannot find it. Based on the lesson, what is the best explanation?

answers.text: The student is using an inaccurate copy of the Constitution
Judicial review is not explicit in Article III's text; the Supreme Court claimed the power for itself in Marbury v. Madison in 1803
Judicial review appears only in the Bill of Rights, not Article III
The phrase was removed from the Constitution by a later amendment

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states directly that judicial review is not written into Article III's text, and that the Supreme Court claimed the power in Marbury v. Madison (1803) rather than exercising an explicitly granted authority.

questions.text: Based on the lesson's summary of Marshall's reasoning in Marbury, which two premises combine to justify a court refusing to enforce an unconstitutional statute?

answers.text: That judges are elected and that Congress is not
That the Constitution is supreme law under Article VI and that courts must resolve conflicts between legal authorities by applying whichever one actually governs
That the President requested the ruling and that Congress agreed in advance
That the statute in question was unpopular with voters

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson traces Marshall's reasoning to the Supremacy Clause (Article VI) establishing the Constitution as supreme law, combined with the judiciary's basic duty to decide which legal rule governs when two conflict; not to popularity, elections, or other-branch approval.

questions.text: A student claims: "Judicial review was a brand-new idea Hamilton and Marshall each invented independently, with no connection between them." Based on the lesson, what is the strongest evidence against this claim?

answers.text: Hamilton and Marshall never discussed the judiciary in their writings
Federalist No. 78 (1788) already argued that "the constitution ought to be preferred to the statute" when the two conflict, fifteen years before Marbury (1803) made the same reasoning operative law
Marshall wrote Federalist No. 78 under a pseudonym
The Constitution explicitly credits Hamilton with inventing judicial review

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson is explicit that Hamilton's 1788 essay contains "essentially unchanged" the same reasoning Marshall used in 1803, describing this as an idea reasoned out and publicly debated well before any court exercised it; not two unrelated inventions.

questions.text: In the Federalist No. 78 excerpt, Hamilton insists judicial review does not make courts "superior" to the legislature. Based on the excerpt, what does he say is actually superior to both?

answers.text: Nothing; Hamilton believed courts were superior to Congress
The power of the people, as declared in the constitution, which is superior to both the judicial and legislative powers
The executive branch, which Hamilton believed should settle all such disputes
Whichever branch has held power the longest

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The excerpt states directly that judicial review "supposes that the power of the people is superior to both" the judiciary and the legislature, and that judges follow the Constitution over a conflicting statute because it reflects "the intention of the people," not because judges outrank lawmakers.

questions.text: Combining Lesson 6.12 and the Federalist No. 78 excerpt, which of the following pairs of later cases does the lesson identify as examples of judicial review in operation, to be studied in more depth later this semester?

answers.text: Marbury v. Madison and the Judiciary Act of 1789
Brown v. Board of Education and Miranda v. Arizona
The Seisachtheia and the reforms of Cleisthenes
Federalist No. 70 and Federalist No. 10

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson names Brown v. Board of Education (1954) and Miranda v. Arizona (1966) as later cases built on the judicial review mechanism established in Marbury, previewed briefly here and reserved for deeper study in a later unit. (a) and (d) name earlier material from this course, not judicial-review cases; (c) refers to Module 1's Athens content.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 7.3: Why a Bill of Rights At All
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts from the lesson. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: Alexander Hamilton argued in Federalist No. 84 that a bill of rights was unnecessary. Based on the lesson, what was the core of his reasoning?

answers.text: Individual rights were unimportant compared to national defense
The federal government could only exercise powers specifically granted to it, so there was no unlimited power left to restrict
The states already had identical bills of rights, making a federal one redundant
Madison had personally promised to add one later, making it unnecessary to write in

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explains Hamilton's argument through the principle of enumerated powers: since the federal government possessed only the powers the Constitution granted it, and no power to restrict speech or religion had been granted, a prohibition against exercising that power was unnecessary.

questions.text: Several states ratified the Constitution in 1788 only after securing an understanding that a bill of rights would follow. What does this tell you about the ratification process?

answers.text: Ratification was unconditional and enthusiastic in every state
The Constitution could not legally be ratified without a bill of rights already attached
Anti-Federalist objections were influential enough to shape the terms on which ratification occurred, even though they lost the larger fight
Madison wrote the Bill of Rights before the Constitution was ratified

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (c). The lesson states the Constitution was ratified "on something close to a promise still owed" after Anti-Federalist pressure in states like Massachusetts, Virginia, and New York secured commitments to add amendments; showing the losing side still shaped the outcome. (b) and (d) contradict the timeline given; (a) contradicts the described conditions.

questions.text: James Madison originally opposed a bill of rights but became its chief drafter. Based on the lesson, which combination of factors best explains this reversal?

answers.text: A political need to satisfy voters in his House race, and Jefferson's argument that a written list would give courts a textual basis to strike down violating laws
A Supreme Court ruling ordering Congress to add one
Hamilton's insistence that enumerated powers were insufficient
Madison's belief that the Constitution's structure was inadequate from the start

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (a). The lesson names two specific causes: Madison's electoral contest against Monroe in a district favoring a bill of rights, and Jefferson's argument (from France) that a written list would equip courts to invalidate violating laws. (d) misstates Madison's original view, which held the structure was already adequate.

questions.text: Madison proposed twelve amendments to the First Congress. Based on the lesson, what happened to the two that were not ratified in 1791?

answers.text: Both were ratified decades later as ordinary amendments
One concerning congressional pay raises was eventually ratified in 1992 as the Twenty-Seventh Amendment; the other, on district size, was never ratified
Both were withdrawn by Madison himself before the states could vote
Both concerned the Bill of Rights's enforcement mechanism

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson specifies that the congressional-pay-raise amendment was ratified in 1992 as the Twenty-Seventh Amendment, while the amendment governing the size of congressional districts was never ratified. Only one of the two, not both, eventually succeeded, ruling out (a).

questions.text: A student claims: "The Ninth and Tenth Amendments protect specific individual liberties, just like the First Amendment does." Based on the lesson, what is the strongest evidence against this claim?

answers.text: The Ninth and Tenth Amendments were never ratified
The Ninth and Tenth Amendments state interpretive principles about how to read the Constitution's grant and reservation of power, rather than naming a specific protected liberty
The First Amendment does not name any specific liberties either
The Ninth and Tenth Amendments apply only to the judiciary

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explicitly distinguishes the Ninth and Tenth from "the first eight" by noting they "work differently"; rather than naming a liberty, the Ninth guards against reading the enumerated list as exhaustive, and the Tenth restates the reservation of unallocated power to the states or the people. (c) misstates the lesson's account of the First Amendment.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 7.11: The Speech Clause and the Case for Free Expression
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts from the lesson. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: A senator proposes a law making it a crime to publish an op-ed arguing that a sitting President should be impeached, on the grounds that the argument is unfair. Based on the lesson's account of self-government, what is the strongest objection to this law?

answers.text: It would violate the Establishment Clause
It would deprive citizens of one of the levers that makes them citizens rather than subjects
It would count as a "true threat" under the narrow exceptions the lesson describes
It would be constitutional because Congress may regulate unfair speech

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson argues that a citizen who cannot criticize the government he is subject to is a subject in fact, not a full citizen, because self-government requires the freedom to judge rulers through public argument. (a) confuses speech with religion; (c) misapplies a narrow exception meant for genuine threats of violence, not unfair argument; (d) contradicts the lesson's central claim.

questions.text: The lesson describes censorship as "a bet that the censor is smarter than the process of argument itself." Which of the following best restates why the classical liberal tradition considers that a bad bet for government to make?

answers.text: Governments are legally forbidden from having opinions
No individual or government reliably knows in advance which contested ideas are true, so open contest is more likely to sort true from false than official suppression
The Constitution requires all ideas to be given equal television time
Speech can never actually cause harm, so there is nothing to bet on

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). This is the lesson's first argument for free speech: reliable judgment of truth at the moment an idea is spoken is not available to any single authority, so open contest is the better mechanism for sorting truth from error over time. (a), (c), and (d) are not claims the lesson makes.

questions.text: A student says a mob leader who deliberately whips up a crowd to attack a bystander immediately, right there in the street, should be able to claim full First Amendment protection because he was "just talking." Based on the lesson, what is the best response?

answers.text: He is correct; all speech, however used, receives full protection

His words likely fall under the narrow "incitement to imminent lawless action" exception, since they were intended to and likely to produce immediate lawless conduct rather than contribute an idea for debate
He is incorrect only because mobs are illegal under the Establishment Clause
He is incorrect because the First Amendment does not apply to speech given outdoors

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson names incitement to imminent lawless action as a narrow category outside full protection precisely because such speech functions as action rather than as an idea offered for testing in debate. (a) contradicts the "not quite absolute" section; (c) and (d) are not real distinctions drawn anywhere in the lesson.

questions.text: Which of the following pairs of ideas does the lesson connect explicitly by tracing them to the same underlying thread studied earlier this semester?

answers.text: The Sedition Act of 1798 and the Establishment Clause
Solon's jury right, Locke's theory of legitimate government, and the requirement that citizens be free to criticize their rulers
The Pentakosiomedimnoi and the Free Exercise Clause
Ostracism and the incitement exception

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explicitly links Solon's jury right and Locke's consent-based theory of government to the free-speech argument, framing all three as expressions of the same idea: a citizen must retain some lever of judgment over the government that rules him. The other pairs are not connected in the lesson.

questions.text: The lesson notes that the founding generation itself passed the Sedition Act of 1798, restricting criticism of government officials, only a few years after ratifying the First Amendment. What point does the lesson use this historical fact to make?

answers.text: That the First Amendment was not seriously meant to protect political speech
That even the founders' own generation was tempted to silence government critics, which is exactly the temptation the free speech guarantee exists to foreclose
That the Sedition Act proves speech protection has always been absolute
That the First Amendment was added only after 1798

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson uses the Sedition Act to show how quickly the temptation to silence critics returns even among people who just wrote a constitutional guarantee against it; illustrating why a binding rule, rather than trust in current majorities, was thought necessary. (a) and (c) misstate the lesson's point, and (d) is chronologically backwards and not asserted.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 7.19: The Fourth and Fifth Amendments
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts from the lesson. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: A colonial customs officer holding a writ of assistance could search a merchant's warehouse without stating what he expected to find there. Which specific clause of the Fourth Amendment was written to prevent exactly this kind of search?

answers.text: The due process clause
The requirement that warrants particularly describe the place and things to be seized
The grand jury clause
The double jeopardy clause

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explains that writs of assistance authorized searching anywhere for anything, and that the Fourth Amendment's particularity requirement is a direct, point-by-point rebuttal of that practice. (a), (c), and (d) are Fifth Amendment protections, not Fourth Amendment search provisions.

questions.text: John Lilburne refused to take the Star Chamber's oath because it would have required him to answer questions about a crime before he even knew the charge against him. Which Fifth Amendment protection traces most directly back to cases like Lilburne's?

answers.text: The grand jury requirement
Protection against double jeopardy
The privilege against self-incrimination
Due process of law

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (c). The lesson identifies Lilburne's 1637 trial as the direct historical origin of the privilege against self-incrimination, since his objection was to being compelled to answer accusatory questions against himself. The other three options are distinct Fifth Amendment guarantees not tied to Lilburne's case in the lesson.

questions.text: Suppose a federal prosecutor, having lost a jury trial, simply files the identical charge against the same defendant for the same offense a second time, hoping for a different jury. Which constitutional guarantee would this violate?

answers.text: The warrant requirement
Double jeopardy
The grand jury clause
Probable cause

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson describes double jeopardy as preventing exactly this scenario; a prosecutor retrying an acquitted or already-tried defendant for the same offense until securing a conviction. The other options concern search procedure or charging procedure, not repeated prosecution.

questions.text: Based on the lesson's account of the writs of assistance and the Star Chamber oath, what structural feature did both historical abuses share?

answers.text: Both required a magistrate's independent approval before the government could act
Both allowed government officials to act against a person without any independent check beforehand
Both applied only to capital crimes
Both were eventually written into the Fourth Amendment's text unchanged

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explicitly draws this parallel: the writs let officials "search first and explain never," and the Star Chamber oath let inquisitors "demand answers first and specify the charge never"; in both cases, no independent check operated before the government acted. (a) describes the American solution, not the abuse itself.

questions.text: A student claims: "The Fourth and Fifth Amendments appear next to each other in the Bill of Rights purely by coincidence of drafting order." Based on the lesson, what is the strongest evidence against this claim?

answers.text: Both amendments were ratified in the same year, 1791
Both amendments respond to the same underlying colonial experience of government acting without prior justification, despite touching different parts of a person's life
Both amendments were written by James Otis
Both amendments require a grand jury before they take effect

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson argues directly that "it is not an accident of drafting" that these amendments sit side by side, because both target the same structural abuse (government acting first and justifying itself never) applied to different domains (the home versus the conscience). (a) is true but does not by itself establish a substantive connection; (c) and (d) are factually incorrect.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 8.3: The Reconstruction Amendments and Plessy v. Ferguson
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts from the lesson. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: The Citizens' Committee in New Orleans deliberately chose Homer Plessy, a man seven-eighths white in appearance, to challenge the Separate Car Act, rather than someone whose race would have been visually obvious to a train conductor. Based on the lesson, what was the strategic purpose of this choice?

answers.text: To make sure Plessy would not be arrested at all
To force the courts to confront the law's racial classification on its own logical terms, rather than let the case turn on visible appearance
To qualify Plessy for a first-class ticket he could not otherwise have purchased
To ensure the case would be dismissed on a technicality

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states the Committee wanted a case that would force the courts to confront the law's logic directly, "not a case complicated by visible appearance"; Plessy's arrest depended on his own statement of his ancestry, not on how he looked.

questions.text: Justice Brown's majority opinion argued that if Black passengers felt Louisiana's law stamped them with a "badge of inferiority," that feeling arose only because Black passengers chose to interpret it that way. Based on the lesson's account of both the majority opinion and the reality of segregation in practice, what is the strongest criticism of this reasoning?

answers.text: The reasoning is correct because the Separate Car Act treated both races identically in every respect

The reasoning locates the injury in the perception of the people the law targeted, rather than in the law's actual design and effect, and in practice "separate" facilities were almost never truly equal
The reasoning was later adopted unanimously by the Supreme Court and remains the law today
The reasoning has no bearing on the case, since Brown's opinion did not discuss badges of inferiority at all

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states plainly that separate facilities were "almost never actually equal" and that Brown's reasoning shifted the source of harm onto Black passengers' own feelings rather than onto the law and the segregated system it authorized.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the constitutional doctrine the majority established in Plessy v. Ferguson?

answers.text: State-mandated racial segregation always violates the Equal Protection Clause
The Equal Protection Clause applies only to the federal government, not the states
State-mandated racial segregation does not violate the Equal Protection Clause as long as the separated facilities are substantially equal
Railroads, but not schools, may be racially segregated under the Fourteenth Amendment

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (c). This is the "separate but equal" doctrine as the lesson states it: segregation is constitutional under the Fourteenth Amendment provided the separated facilities are nominally equal. The Fourteenth Amendment binds the states directly (ruling out b), and the majority's reasoning was not limited to railroads (ruling out d).

questions.text: Justice Harlan compared the majority's decision in Plessy to the Court's ruling in the Dred Scott case. Based on the lesson, what point was Harlan most likely making with that comparison?

answers.text: That both cases involved railroad regulation
That the Court was, in his view, repeating a historic constitutional failure by upholding a law built on racial hierarchy
That Dred Scott had already been overturned by the Fourteenth Amendment, making the comparison purely historical
That both decisions were popular with the public at the time they were issued

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson frames Harlan's Dred Scott comparison as "a direct, pointed comparison to the Court's other great constitutional failure"; Harlan was warning that the Court was about to repeat, in a new form, the kind of decision that denied full citizenship and equality on the basis of race.

questions.text: The lesson states that the Reconstruction Amendments were written for a specific purpose regarding the roughly four million people freed by the Thirteenth Amendment. Given that purpose, and given the majority's holding in Plessy, why does the lesson characterize Plessy as a case in which the Fourteenth Amendment failed to do the work it was written for?

answers.text: Because the Fourteenth Amendment was written to guarantee full and equal citizenship, and the Court instead used its Equal Protection Clause to bless a law separating citizens by race
Because the Fourteenth Amendment does not mention citizenship at all
Because Louisiana refused to recognize the Fourteenth Amendment as valid law
Because the case was decided before the Fourteenth Amendment was ratified

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (a). The lesson explains the Reconstruction Amendments were meant to make freed citizens citizens "in fact, not merely in name," while the Plessy majority read the Equal Protection Clause as permitting exactly the kind of state-mandated racial separation those amendments were written to foreclose.

This final module turns the question around: it studies the duties citizens owe the republic in return; voting, jury service, military service; the foreign policy the republic conducts in the world, and, in its final week, the governments that recognize no constitutional limit on power at all. Restate your current answer in two or three sentences, and predict: does a constitution's real strength lie more in what it stops government from doing, or in what it asks citizens to do?

This module you'll study the civic duties of voting, jury service, and military service, the major theories behind American foreign policy, and how totalitarian governments in the twentieth century operated with no constitutional check at all. Which are you most curious about right now?

answers.text: Voting, juries, and military service
U.S. foreign policy theories and wars
Communism, totalitarianism, and unchecked power

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 9.3: Civic Duties: Voting, Juries, and Military Service
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts from the lesson. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: A citizen who ignores a jury summons and a citizen who simply never registers to vote face very different legal consequences. Based on the lesson, what best explains this difference?

answers.text: Voting is a state duty and jury service is a federal duty
Jury service is a legally enforceable duty, while voting is a civic expectation without a legal penalty for non-participation
Jury service was only made mandatory after the 26th Amendment
There is no real difference; both carry equal fines

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states no U.S. law compels voting, while ignoring a jury summons can bring contempt charges, fines, or jail. The distinction is legal enforceability, not level of government (ruling out a) or amendment history (ruling out c).

questions.text: A 16-year-old in Florida completes voter preregistration paperwork. Based on the lesson, what happens as a direct result?

answers.text: She may vote immediately in any local election
Her registration automatically activates when she turns 18
She is exempted from future jury service
Nothing happens until she reapplies at 18

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explains preregistration lets 16- and 17-year-olds complete the paperwork in advance so registration activates automatically on their 18th birthday; not immediately (ruling out a) and without needing to reapply (ruling out d). Jury exemption is never mentioned (ruling out c).

questions.text: The lesson argues that jury service is "the necessary flip side" of the 6th Amendment jury-trial right. Which statement best captures why?

answers.text: The 6th Amendment requires defendants to serve on their own juries
A defendant's right to a jury of peers can only be honored if other citizens fulfill the duty of staffing that jury
The 6th Amendment only applies to civil, not criminal, cases
Jury service was added to the Constitution by the 7th Amendment

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson's core claim is that a right held by one party (the defendant) depends on a duty performed by others (the jury pool). (a) and (d) misstate the amendments; (c) reverses which amendment covers criminal versus civil trials.

questions.text: Based on the lesson, which best describes the relationship between Selective Service registration and military conscription?

answers.text: They are the same legal requirement under a different name
Registration is the preparedness list; conscription is the compulsory service the government has reserved the right to activate from that list
Registration only applies during an active draft
Conscription has never actually been used in U.S. history

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson describes registration as an ongoing peacetime requirement distinct from actual compulsory service, which the lesson states has been activated in the Civil War, both World Wars, Korea, and Vietnam; directly contradicting (d) and (c).

questions.text: A student claims: "All three civic duties covered in this lesson are enforced the same way; through culture and expectation, not law." Based on the lesson, what is the strongest evidence against this claim?

answers.text: Voting requires preregistration in Florida
Ignoring a jury summons can result in contempt of court, fines, or jail; a legal penalty voting does not carry
Military service is entirely voluntary in the United States
The Constitution never mentions juries

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explicitly contrasts jury duty's legal enforceability with voting's reliance on civic expectation alone, disproving the claim that all three duties are enforced identically. (a) is true but doesn't address enforcement mechanism; (c) and (d) misstate the lesson.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 9.11: Five Theories of American Foreign Policy
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts from the lesson. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: A senator in the 1840s argues that the United States has a right, even an obligation, to settle the continent "from sea to sea," but says nothing about intervening in European affairs. Which single label best captures this senator's position as described?

answers.text: Isolationist only
Realist only
Expansionist, with no necessary position on European entanglement
Idealist only

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (c). The lesson explains that expansionism concerns growth (here, continental growth under Manifest Destiny) and can coexist with isolationism regarding Europe, since the two postures answer different questions. The senator's statement, as given, is a growth claim, not a statement about foreign alliances one way or the other.

questions.text: Washington's Farewell Address warns against "permanent alliances" but explicitly allows for "temporary alliances for extraordinary emergencies." Based on the lesson, what does this distinction tell you about isolationism as a category?

answers.text: Isolationism requires total withdrawal from all foreign contact, including trade
Isolationism opposes binding, long-term political and military commitments, not all foreign engagement
Isolationism was abandoned immediately after Washington's presidency
Isolationism and expansionism are logically incompatible

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson states isolationist statesmen generally still favored trade and diplomacy, and resisted specifically binding political and military commitment. Washington's own carve-out for temporary emergency alliances confirms this. (a), (c), and (d) all overstate or misstate the lesson.

questions.text: The Monroe Doctrine declared European colonization or interference in the Western Hemisphere an act hostile to the United States, without proposing that the U.S. annex or govern Latin American nations directly. Which category does this best illustrate?

answers.text: Expansionism, because it involves territory
Sphere of influence, because it claims a whole region as a zone of primary interest without annexing it
Isolationism, because it excludes Europe
Realism only, with no idealist element at all

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson defines a sphere of influence as a claimed zone of primary interest short of annexation, and names the Monroe Doctrine as the founding American example of exactly this pattern. (a) is wrong because no territorial annexation is proposed; (c) misreads the Doctrine as excluding rather than claiming a hemisphere; (d) contradicts the lesson's explicit note that Monroe's claim was partly justified in idealist terms.

questions.text: A policymaker allies the United States with a government she privately considers repressive, because the alliance strengthens American security against a more dangerous rival power. Based on the lesson's definitions, which posture is she primarily exercising in this decision?

answers.text: Idealism, because she is thinking about values
Isolationism, because she is avoiding conflict
Realism, because she is calculating national interest and power rather than acting on moral ideals as such
Expansionism, because an alliance expands American reach

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (c). The lesson defines realism as decision-making based on calculated national interest and power, "regardless of whether the methods or the partners involved are especially admirable"; precisely the scenario described. (a) is the opposite of what's described; (b) and (d) mischaracterize an alliance decision made for strategic reasons.

questions.text: The lesson states that the Monroe Doctrine "was justified partly in the idealist language of protecting hemispheric self-government from European monarchy." What broader point about these five categories does this example support?

answers.text: Idealism and spheres of influence are mutually exclusive categories
Real foreign-policy episodes are usually blends of more than one category, not pure instances of a single one
The Monroe Doctrine should be reclassified as pure idealism
Realist and idealist justifications can never appear in the same policy

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson's closing section argues explicitly that almost no real episode is a pure specimen of one category, and uses the Monroe Doctrine (sphere-of-influence claim justified partly in idealist language) as one of its two supporting examples. (a), (c), and (d) all contradict this point.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz 9.19: Communism as a Governmental and Economic System
quizzes.description: 5 multiple-choice questions. No question is answerable by locating a single sentence; each requires connecting two or more facts from the lesson. Answer key and rationale included below for teacher reference; students see only the questions and (after submission) their score.

questions.text: A student claims: "Marx's own theory predicted that centralized state power would grow stronger and more permanent over time." Based on the lesson, what is the strongest evidence against this claim?

answers.text: Marx never wrote about the state at all
Marx's theory held that once class conflict ended, the state itself would become unnecessary and "wither away"
Marx argued the state should be abolished immediately by revolution
Marx believed only a monarchy could achieve a classless society

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explicitly notes that Marx's theoretical endpoint involved the state "withering away" once no ruling-class interest remained to protect, directly contradicting a claim that his theory predicted permanent, growing state power. (a), (c), and (d) are not supported by the lesson.

questions.text: Under the Soviet command economy, who determined how much steel or grain would be produced in a given year?

answers.text: Independent buyers and sellers responding to market prices
Centralized state planning agencies setting targets from Moscow
Regional courts ruling on production disputes
A rotating council elected by factory workers each year

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson describes Soviet planning agencies setting five-year targets centrally, explicitly without the price signals a market economy relies on. (a) describes the opposite system; (c) and (d) are not mentioned.

questions.text: The lesson distinguishes an "authoritarian" government from a "totalitarian" one. Based on that distinction, which of the following would be the clearest sign a government has crossed from authoritarian into totalitarian?

answers.text: The government bans one opposition newspaper but leaves private businesses alone
The government fuses control of politics, the economy, and cultural and personal life under one party and ideology
The government holds elections only every six years instead of every four
The government raises taxes on private industry

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson defines totalitarianism specifically as control extending beyond politics into the whole of economic, cultural, and personal life, with no private sphere left standing; the fusion described in (b). (a), (c), and (d) describe narrower authoritarian measures, not the total fusion the lesson defines.

questions.text: Soviet show trials of the 1930s featured defendants confessing to crimes against the state after coerced interrogation. Based on the lesson's comparison to the American judiciary, what specific constitutional safeguard was absent in this process?

answers.text: A two-thirds vote requirement in the Senate
Judicial independence; courts able to rule against the government without fear of retaliation
The Three-Fifths Compromise
The Necessary and Proper Clause

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson explicitly names judicial independence, tied to Article III's lifetime tenure protections, as the safeguard absent when Soviet judges served at the Party's pleasure and show trials functioned as political theater rather than impartial law. (a), (c), and (d) are unrelated provisions from earlier in the course.

questions.text: The Soviet constitution of 1936 listed rights resembling the American Bill of Rights. Based on the lesson, why does it argue these rights did not function as genuine constitutional constraints on the government?

answers.text: The rights were never written down at all
No independent court, free press, or competing political power existed to enforce those rights against the party that had granted them
The rights applied only to Communist Party members
The Soviet constitution was never ratified

questions.feedback_general: Answer: (b). The lesson's central claim is that a right is only a real constraint if some power independent of the government can enforce it; since Soviet courts, press, and politics were all controlled by the same party the rights were meant to restrain, the rights functioned as unenforceable promises rather than constraints. (a), (c), and (d) are not stated in the lesson.

Built natively in Canvas Quizzes (survey mode); no custom code. Reproduced here as question text for the master document.

How does a constitution built on paper actually constrain power in practice, and what happens when it doesn't?

You have now studied all three branches of the federal government, civil liberties and civil rights cases, the civic duties citizens owe the republic, American foreign policy across the Cold War, and, this session, what happens when a government recognizes no constitutional limit on its power at all.
