discussions.title: Critical Questions 1.5
discussions.html:
Critical Questions 1.5

Directions: Answer each question in a well-developed paragraph, citing specific language from the excerpt. There is no single correct answer to most of these; you are graded on the quality of your reasoning, not on reaching a predetermined conclusion.

1. Aristotle reports that Solon's critics accused him of personally profiting from the Seisachtheia by tipping off wealthy friends before the debt cancellation was announced. Aristotle argues this charge is not credible. Summarize his argument in your own words. Do you find it convincing? Why or why not?

2. Aristotle singles out the citizen's right to appeal to a court of his peers as more important than the debt cancellation itself. Explain, in your own words, why a right to appeal might matter more, over time, than a one-time relief from debt.

3. Aristotle writes that "when the people is master of the vote, it becomes master of the government." What theory of political legitimacy is embedded in that sentence: that is, what does it assume makes a government's authority rightful in the first place? Name the underlying principle, and explain how the jury right embodies it.

4. Suppose Solon had accepted one of the offers made to him and become the outright champion of either the rich or the poor, ruling by decree instead of writing a constitution he then walked away from. Would Athens likely have developed the same tradition of citizen appeal and jury right on its own, given enough time, or was Solon's personal refusal to rule a necessary condition for that tradition to take hold? Defend your answer with reasoning, not just assertion.

discussions.title: Critical Questions 1.13
discussions.html:
Critical Questions 1.13

Directions: Answer each question in a well-developed paragraph, citing specific language from the excerpt. There is no single correct answer to most of these; you are graded on the quality of your reasoning, not on reaching a predetermined conclusion.

1. Cicero defines "the people" not as any crowd of persons but as a multitude "bound together by the compact of justice, and the communication of utility." What is he ruling out with this definition? Give an example of a large group of people that would not count as "a people" under Cicero's definition, and explain why.

2. Cicero says pure monarchy, pure aristocracy, and pure democracy each tend to "degenerate into something corrupt"; monarchs into despots, aristocracies into "factious oligarchies," and popular rule into "a mob and a hubbub." Choose one of these three degenerations and explain, in your own words, the mechanism Cicero seems to have in mind: what is it about concentrating power in that particular form that invites its corruption?

3. Cicero argues that in the mixed constitution, "there exists no cause of revolution where every one is firmly established in his appropriate station." What theory of political stability is embedded in that claim; that is, what does Cicero assume causes revolutions in the first place, such that distributing power among stations would prevent them? Name the underlying principle and explain how the dual consulship you read about in Lesson 1.10 embodies it.

4. Suppose the Romans of 509 BC had responded to Tarquin's expulsion not by dividing executive power between two annual consuls, but by electing a single powerful magistrate for a long fixed term (say, ten years) reasoning that one capable leader chosen by the people would be more decisive than two colleagues who could veto each other. Using Cicero's argument about why pure forms of government "degenerate," argue for or against this claim: "A single ten-year magistrate, even one elected rather than born to the office, would eventually have reproduced the very problem Rome had just overthrown." Defend your position with specific reasoning, not just assertion.

discussions.title: Critical Questions 2.5
discussions.html:
Critical Questions 2.5

Directions: Answer each question in a well-developed paragraph, citing specific language from the excerpt. There is no single correct answer to most of these; you are graded on the quality of your reasoning, not on reaching a predetermined conclusion.

1. Locke describes the state of nature as governed already by "a law of nature," which teaches that "no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions." Compare this directly to Hobbes's state of nature from Monday's lesson. Is Locke describing the same starting condition Hobbes described, or something different? Be specific about what changes and what, if anything, stays the same.

2. Locke lists three things "wanting" in the state of nature; a settled law, a known judge, and the power to enforce a sentence. Notice that none of these three is "a law telling people how to behave." Explain in your own words why this omission matters: what does Locke seem to think government is actually for, based on this list?

3. Locke says people in the state of nature already possess rights to "life, health, liberty, or possessions" before any government exists. What theory of the origin of rights is embedded in that claim; that is, where do rights come from, on Locke's account, if not from government? Name the underlying principle and explain how it differs from a theory in which government is the source of people's rights.

4. Suppose Locke had agreed with Hobbes that the state of nature is a war of every man against every man, with no natural law restraining anyone. Could Locke still have arrived at a social contract that people could rightfully break if their ruler betrayed them, or does his entire later argument for a "conditional" contract depend on starting from a state of nature that is orderly rather than violent? Defend your answer with reasoning, not just assertion.

discussions.title: Critical Questions 2.13
discussions.html:
Critical Questions 2.13

Directions: Answer each question in a well-developed paragraph, citing specific language from the excerpt. There is no single correct answer to most of these; you are graded on the quality of your reasoning, not on reaching a predetermined conclusion.

1. Montesquieu writes that political liberty is "a tranquillity of mind arising from the opinion each person has of his safety." Explain, in your own words, why he defines liberty this way (as a feeling of safety) rather than as, say, the ability to do whatever you want. What does this definition assume liberty is actually protecting people from?

2. Montesquieu says that "there would be an end of every thing" if the same body held all three powers, whether that body is made up of "the nobles or of the people." Why does he insist this danger applies just as much to a body of ordinary people as to a body of aristocrats? What does that tell you about whether Montesquieu thinks democracy, by itself, guarantees liberty?

3. Montesquieu's proposed solution is that "power should be a check to power." Name this principle in the vocabulary this lesson used to describe it, and explain how the specific example of the executive's veto and the legislature's control of funding illustrates the principle at work, rather than simply restating it.

4. Suppose Montesquieu had visited France instead of England when forming his admiration for a working constitution, and suppose eighteenth-century France had, in fact, united all three powers in the king's person, with no separate legislature or independent courts at all. Would Montesquieu likely have arrived at the same theory of separated powers purely through abstract reasoning, without a real working example to point to? Or was the existence of an actual (if imperfect) English model necessary for him to develop and defend the argument as persuasively as he did? Defend your answer with reasoning, not just assertion.

discussions.title: Critical Questions 3.5
discussions.html:
Critical Questions 3.5

Directions: Answer each question in a well-developed paragraph, citing specific language from the excerpt. There is no single correct answer to most of these; you are graded on the quality of your reasoning, not on reaching a predetermined conclusion.

1. The Declaration states that governments derive "their just powers from the consent of the governed," and that when government becomes "destructive of these ends," the people have both a right and a duty to "alter or to abolish it." In your own words, restate this argument, and explain how the long list of grievances against George III that follows is meant to satisfy the conditions this sentence sets.

2. Notice that the Declaration also cautions that "governments long established should not be changed for light and transient causes," and that "mankind are more disposed to suffer… than to right themselves." Why do you think Jefferson included this caution about hasty rebellion in a document whose entire purpose is to justify a rebellion? What work does this sentence do for the document's credibility?

3. The Declaration's second paragraph is applying a specific philosophical theory of government to justify separation. Name the theory and the philosopher whose work it draws from most directly, and explain precisely how the sentence "governments are instituted among men, deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed" reflects that philosopher's account of why and how legitimate government arises.

4. Suppose Thomas Paine's Common Sense had never been published, and no comparably persuasive case against monarchy had circulated in early 1776. Would the Continental Congress likely still have declared independence that summer, or would the political mood have more likely stayed at the level of "redress of grievances" for longer? Defend your answer with reasoning about what Paine's argument specifically supplied that the colonies' decade of complaints about taxation had not.

discussions.title: Critical Questions 4.5
discussions.html:
Critical Questions 4.5

Directions: Answer each question in a well-developed paragraph, citing specific language from the excerpt. There is no single correct answer to most of these; you are graded on the quality of your reasoning, not on reaching a predetermined conclusion.

1. The Preamble opens with "We the People," not "We the States." Given what you read in Monday's lesson about Madison's diagnosis of the Articles' central weakness; a confederacy's inability to act directly on individual citizens; explain why that opening phrase is not simply ceremonial language, but a direct statement of the new government's theory of its own authority.

2. Article V sets different thresholds for proposing an amendment (two-thirds) and ratifying one (three-fourths). Why might the framers have wanted ratification to be harder than proposal, rather than setting both at the same threshold?

3. Article V makes the Constitution amendable by procedures embedded within the document itself, rather than treating the Constitution as fixed for all time or subject to change only by another revolution. What theory of constitutional legitimacy is at work here; that is, what does building in a formal amendment process assume about where a constitution's authority ultimately comes from, and about the relationship between one generation's laws and the next generation's consent? Name the assumption and explain how Article V embodies it.

4. Suppose the framers had written Article V to require unanimous consent of all the states for any amendment, exactly as the Articles of Confederation had required. Based on what you know about why the Articles proved unfixable, argue for or against this claim: "A Constitution amendable only by unanimous consent would have collapsed, or been abandoned, within a generation." Defend your position with specific reasoning, not just assertion.

discussions.title: Critical Questions 4.13
discussions.html:
Critical Questions 4.13

Directions: Answer each question in a well-developed paragraph, citing specific language from the excerpt. There is no single correct answer to most of these; you are graded on the quality of your reasoning, not on reaching a predetermined conclusion.

1. Madison writes that liberty is "to faction, what air is to fire." Explain this analogy in your own words. What is Madison arguing about the relationship between freedom and faction, and why does that relationship rule out destroying liberty as a solution?

2. Madison distinguishes a faction that is a minority from one that is a majority. Why does he treat majority faction as the more serious danger to a republic, even though majorities are usually understood to be the legitimate rulers in a democracy?

3. Madison's argument for the extended republic implicitly rejects the idea (central to Rousseau's theory of the general will, which you studied in Module 2) that a unified political community can discover and act on a single common good if it stays small and direct. Name the underlying disagreement between Madison and Rousseau about human nature or political community, and explain how No. 10's argument for size and diversity follows from Madison's side of that disagreement.

4. Suppose the United States in 1787 had been a small, homogeneous nation (one state, one dominant economic interest, one dominant religion) rather than a diverse confederation of thirteen states. Would Madison's argument for an extended republic have applied in the same way? Would his recommended solution to the problem of faction still have worked, or would it have needed to be different? Defend your answer with reasoning drawn from the text, not just assertion.

discussions.title: Critical Questions 4.21
discussions.html:
Critical Questions 4.21

Directions: Answer each question in a well-developed paragraph, citing specific language from the excerpt. There is no single correct answer to most of these; you are graded on the quality of your reasoning, not on reaching a predetermined conclusion.

1. Hamilton claims the system "unites in an eminent degree all the advantages, the union of which was to be wished for." List at least three distinct advantages he claims the Electoral College achieves simultaneously. Does listing them together make his case more or less convincing to you, and why?

2. Hamilton warns specifically about foreign powers trying to raise "a creature of their own to the chief magistracy of the union." Explain, in your own words, exactly how the design of the Electoral College (as Hamilton describes it) was meant to make this harder to accomplish than it would have been under direct popular election or legislative selection.

3. Hamilton's argument rests on a claim about the difference between a large, dispersed mass of voters and a small, deliberative body of chosen representatives. Name the underlying political principle at work here (the idea that certain decisions are better made by a filtered, deliberative body than by a direct popular vote), and explain where else in this course (or in the structure of the Constitution generally) you have seen the framers apply that same principle.

4. Suppose the framers had adopted direct national popular election of the president instead of the Electoral College, but eighteenth-century America had somehow already possessed instant, reliable, nationwide communication (imagine, for the sake of argument, that every voter could learn everything relevant about every candidate within a day). Would Hamilton's objections to direct election still apply with the same force? Which of his four stated goals would be satisfied by instant communication, and which would remain unaddressed regardless? Defend your answer with reasoning drawn from the text.

discussions.title: Critical Questions 7.5
discussions.html:
Critical Questions 7.5

Directions: Answer each question in a well-developed paragraph, citing specific language from the excerpt. There is no single correct answer to most of these; you are graded on the quality of your reasoning, not on reaching a predetermined conclusion.

1. The First Amendment protects religion, speech, the press, assembly, and petition in a single sentence. Why might the framers have grouped these five particular freedoms together, rather than treating each as a separate amendment? What do they have in common as a category of right?

2. The Third Amendment, forbidding the quartering of soldiers in private homes without consent, is rarely litigated today. Using what you know from Lesson 7.2 about why the Bill of Rights was written, explain why the framers still thought it important enough to include.

3. The Fourth Amendment requires that warrants issue only "upon probable cause" and must "particularly describe" the place and things to be searched. What underlying principle about the relationship between citizen and government is this specificity requirement designed to protect; that is, what is it guarding against, in principle, beyond the literal case of an unwanted house search? Name the principle and explain how the amendment's wording embodies it.

4. Suppose Hamilton had won the argument in Federalist No. 84, and the First Congress had never proposed a bill of rights at all. Given the enumerated-powers structure the Constitution already provided, would Americans' First and Fourth Amendment freedoms most likely have ended up roughly as well protected anyway through ordinary lawmaking and litigation, or does something depend specifically on these rights having been written into the Constitution's text? Defend your answer with reasoning, not just assertion.

discussions.title: Critical Questions 7.13
discussions.html:
Critical Questions 7.13

Directions: Answer each question in a well-developed paragraph, citing specific language from the excerpt. There is no single correct answer to most of these; you are graded on the quality of your reasoning, not on reaching a predetermined conclusion.

1. Chief Justice Burger writes that the three-part test asks whether a law has a secular purpose, whether its primary effect neither advances nor inhibits religion, and whether it avoids "excessive government entanglement with religion." Restate the third prong (entanglement) in your own words. Why might a law that passes the first two parts of the test still fail on entanglement grounds?

2. The Court argues that a textbook's content can be checked once, but "a teacher's handling of a subject" cannot, and that ensuring teachers stay strictly secular would require "comprehensive, discriminating, and continuing state surveillance." Do you find this distinction between books and teachers persuasive as a reason to treat the two forms of aid differently under the Establishment Clause? Why or why not?

3. The opinion states that "political division along religious lines was one of the principal evils against which the First Amendment was intended to protect." What underlying concern about religion and republican self-government is the Court expressing here; that is, what does the Court fear happens to a political community when its elections and legislatures start splitting along religious lines rather than on ordinary political questions? Connect your answer to the reasons this course has studied for why the founders wanted government kept out of the business of favoring one religious group over another.

4. Suppose Pennsylvania and Rhode Island had instead funneled the aid to parents rather than to the schools (for instance, by giving a education tax credit that parents could use to pay tuition anywhere, public or private, religious or not) rather than paying schools directly for teacher salaries. Would the entanglement problem the Court identifies in Lemon still apply with the same force? Defend your answer with reasoning about what specifically produced the entanglement in the case as decided.

discussions.title: Critical Questions 7.21
discussions.html:
Critical Questions 7.21

Directions: Answer each question in a well-developed paragraph, citing specific language from the excerpt. There is no single correct answer to most of these; you are graded on the quality of your reasoning, not on reaching a predetermined conclusion.

1. The Court writes that the "atmosphere and environment of incommunicado interrogation as it exists today is inherently intimidating." Notice that the Court reaches this conclusion without alleging that Miranda was beaten, threatened, or physically mistreated in any way. Explain, in your own words, what the Court believes is coercive about custodial interrogation even when no physical force is used at all.

2. The Court requires that a suspect be warned of his rights before any questioning begins, rather than leaving it to a judge to later decide, case by case, whether a given confession was voluntary. What practical problem with the older, case-by-case approach might have led the Court to prefer a fixed, advance requirement instead?

3. The Court grounds its holding in the Fifth Amendment's privilege against self-incrimination, yet the required warnings also include a right to an attorney; a guarantee that appears not in the Fifth Amendment but in the Sixth. What does this pairing suggest about how the Court views the relationship between the right to remain silent and the right to counsel during interrogation? Name the underlying reasoning and explain it in your own words.

4. Suppose the Court, instead of requiring warnings before questioning begins, had simply directed trial judges to more carefully scrutinize confessions after the fact for signs of coercion, using the same "totality of the circumstances" approach the Court had used in the decades before Miranda. Would this alternative have offered suspects like Miranda meaningfully similar protection, or does the timing of the safeguard (before questioning versus after a confession is already in hand) make a real difference? Defend your answer with reasoning, not just assertion.

discussions.title: Critical Questions 8.5
discussions.html:
Critical Questions 8.5

Directions: Answer each question in a well-developed paragraph, citing specific language from the excerpt. There is no single correct answer to most of these; you are graded on the quality of your reasoning, not on reaching a predetermined conclusion.

1. Justice Brown writes that the "underlying fallacy" of Plessy's argument is the assumption that enforced separation "stamps the colored race with a badge of inferiority," and that any such feeling exists "solely because the colored race chooses to put that construction upon it." Restate this argument in your own words, and then explain, using what you know from the lesson about the actual conditions of segregated facilities, why this argument does not hold up as a description of reality.

2. Harlan writes that "every one knows" the Separate Car Act's true purpose was to exclude Black passengers from white train cars, not the reverse. What kind of evidence would you need to decide whether Harlan is right that everyone, including the majority, actually understood this at the time? Does the majority opinion itself give you any evidence either way?

3. Harlan writes that "our Constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens." What theory of equal citizenship is embedded in that sentence; that is, what does it claim the Constitution requires of laws that classify people by race, regardless of whether the classification is framed as "separate but equal"? Explain how this theory differs from the majority's theory of what the Equal Protection Clause requires.

4. Suppose Harlan's dissent had instead been the majority opinion in 1896; that is, suppose the Supreme Court had ruled in Plessy that state-mandated racial segregation violates the Fourteenth Amendment. Would this likely have prevented the rise of Jim Crow segregation across the South in the decades that followed, or would segregation have continued to spread through other means despite an adverse ruling? Defend your answer with reasoning about what a Supreme Court decision can and cannot accomplish by itself.

discussions.title: Critical Questions 9.5
discussions.html:
Critical Questions 9.5

Directions: Answer each question in a well-developed paragraph, citing specific language from the excerpt. There is no single correct answer to most of these; you are graded on the quality of your reasoning, not on reaching a predetermined conclusion.

1. Roosevelt's speech is built almost entirely out of a chronological list of facts; what happened, where, and in what order; rather than an extended argument. Why might a president facing a request this large (a formal declaration of war) choose a plain factual recitation over an emotional or philosophical appeal? What effect does that choice have on the listener?

2. Roosevelt says he believes he is interpreting "the will of the Congress and of the people" in pledging that Japan's "treachery shall never again endanger us." What is he claiming about the relationship between a president's judgment and the public's will at this moment? Is that claim easier or harder to defend in the days immediately following an attack than it would be months later? Explain.

3. Roosevelt asks Congress, not the President himself, to declare that "a state of war has existed" between the United States and Japan. What constitutional principle about the distribution of war powers is he honoring by phrasing his request this way, rather than simply announcing that the United States is at war? Name the principle and the constitutional provision behind it.

4. Suppose the attack on Pearl Harbor had been a smaller, less destructive raid with few American casualties, rather than the devastating strike it actually was. Would Congress likely have granted a declaration of war just as quickly and unanimously, or would the civic sense of a shared, existential threat that this module's lesson connects to broad public support for the WWII draft have been substantially weaker? Defend your answer with reasoning, not just assertion.

discussions.title: Critical Questions 9.13
discussions.html:
Critical Questions 9.13

Directions: Answer each question in a well-developed paragraph, citing specific language from the excerpt. There is no single correct answer to most of these; you are graded on the quality of your reasoning, not on reaching a predetermined conclusion.

1. Truman states plainly that "the Government of Greece is not perfect" and that it "has made mistakes," even as he asks Congress to fund and arm it. Why might a president make this admission out loud, in a speech meant to persuade Congress to spend $400 million? What does this tell you about how Truman wanted the aid request understood?

2. Truman says "it is necessary only to glance at a map" to see why Greece matters to a "much wider situation," warning that Greece's fall could spread "confusion and disorder" through the Middle East and discourage other nations struggling to stay free. Explain, in your own words, the chain of consequences Truman is describing here, and why he thinks a small country's fate can determine the fate of countries far away.

3. Using this module's five-category framework (isolationism, expansionism, spheres of influence, realism, idealism), identify the two categories most clearly at work in this speech and explain how each shows up in Truman's own language. Is one category doing more of the actual persuasive work than the other? Defend your answer with specific quotations.

4. Suppose Truman had asked Congress for aid to Greece and Turkey using only the language of national security and strategic calculation (the Middle East, the map, the danger to American interests), and had left out entirely the language of "free peoples" and "alternative ways of life." Would Congress and the American public likely have supported the request as readily? Would the resulting policy of containment have unfolded the same way over the following decades, or would something about it have been different? Defend your answer with reasoning, not just assertion.

discussions.title: Critical Questions 9.21
discussions.html:
Critical Questions 9.21

Directions: Answer each question in a well-developed paragraph, citing specific details from the reading. There is no single correct answer to most of these; you are graded on the quality of your reasoning, not on reaching a predetermined conclusion.

1. Jones reported what he personally saw and was told by villagers; the Soviet government denied that any extraordinary famine existed at all. Explain, using what you know from Lesson 9.18 about the fusion of political and economic power in the Soviet state, why that government had both the motive and the capacity to suppress this information so effectively.

2. Several Western correspondents based in Moscow downplayed or dismissed Jones's reporting, in part because their own continued access depended on the Soviet government's goodwill. What does this tell you about the conditions a free press needs in order to actually check government power, and what happens to that check when a government controls journalists' access?

3. This course has repeatedly used the idea that rights are only real constraints on government when some power independent of the government can enforce them. Identify the specific "independent power" that was missing in the Soviet Union's handling of the famine; the thing that, had it existed, might have forced the state to respond differently to what Jones reported. Name it and explain how its absence connects to Lesson 9.18's argument.

4. Suppose the Soviet Union in the early 1930s had possessed a free press and an independent judiciary of the kind studied throughout this course. Would the famine itself likely have been prevented entirely, or only reported and responded to differently once it began? Defend your answer with reasoning about what a free press and independent courts can and cannot actually do in the face of a policy already in motion.
